quiz.explanation: The striker strikes the unnotched face directly behind the notch, putting the notch root into severe triaxial tension.

quiz.question: The maximum allowable time to transfer the specimen from conditioning bath to hammer release is:
quiz.explanation: ASTM E23 strictly limits transfer and impact time to within 5 seconds to prevent temperature drift.

quiz.question: A steel fracture surface exhibiting a bright, shiny, crystalline facet appearance indicates:
quiz.explanation: Shiny crystalline facets indicate transgranular brittle cleavage along crystallographic planes with minimal energy absorption.

theory:
1. Fracture Mechanics & High Strain Rate Dynamics

In structural civil engineering, sudden impact loads from vehicle collisions, seismic shockwaves, and wave slap subject structural steel to immense strain rates ($\dot{\varepsilon} \approx 10^2\text{ to }10^4\text{ s}^{-1}$). Under dynamic loading, dislocation velocity is constrained by thermal drag and phonon scattering, raising effective yield strength $\sigma_y^{dyn}$ by up to $100\%$ compared to quasi-static values.

The standard Charpy V-notch specimen ($10 \times 10 \times 55\text{ mm}$) incorporates a sharp notch with root radius $\rho = 0.25\text{ mm}$ and notch depth $a = 2.0\text{ mm}$. Under third-point impact loading across span $S = 40\text{ mm}$, the notch generates plastic slip-line fields described by Hill's slip-line field theory for a notched bar in bending. The elastic stress concentration factor $K_t$ reaches:

\[ K_t = 1 + 2 \sqrt{\frac{a}{\rho}} = 1 + 2 \sqrt{\frac{2.0}{0.25}} = 1 + 2(2.828) \approx 6.66 \]

yielding triaxial tension where hydrostatic tensile stress $\sigma_m = (\sigma_1 + \sigma_2 + \sigma_3)/3$ reaches maximum intensity directly ahead of the notch root.

2. The Ductile-to-Brittle Transition Temperature (DBTT)

Cleavage fracture occurs when local maximum principal stress $\sigma_1$ reaches the temperature-independent critical cleavage fracture stress $\sigma_f^*$. Because plastic yield stress $\sigma_y(T)$ increases exponentially as temperature decreases following Arrhenius kinetics:

\[ \sigma_y(T) = \sigma_0 + C \cdot \exp\left( -\frac{Q}{k_B T} \right) \]

a crossover occurs at the Ductile-to-Brittle Transition Temperature (DBTT). Above DBTT, extensive plastic blunting precedes shear void coalescence (Upper Shelf, $K_V > 80\text{ J}$). Below DBTT, cleavage triggers before plastic blunting (Lower Shelf, $K_V < 15\text{ J}$).

3. Linear Impact Toughness Response Model

Across the linear transition regime ($T = -30^\circ\text{C to }+50^\circ\text{C}$), absorbed impact energy $K_V$ exhibits a linear response:

\[ K_V(T) = k_T \cdot T + K_{V0} \]

where $k_T = 0.8500\text{ J/}^\circ\text{C}$ represents temperature sensitivity, and $K_{V0} = 65.00\text{ J}$ is absorbed energy at $0^\circ\text{C}$.
report:
1. Objective & Practical Significance

The primary objective of this civil engineering laboratory investigation is to determine the Charpy V-notch absorbed impact energy ($K_V$) and evaluate the ductile-to-brittle transition response of ASTM A572 Grade 50 structural bridge steel across five test temperatures ($-30, -10, +10, +30,$ and $+50^\circ\text{C}$) according to ASTM E23 / ISO 148-1. By measuring absorbed energy, lateral expansion, and fracture face morphology, we calibrate the temperature sensitivity slope $k_T$ and verify fracture-critical toughness criteria for bridge engineering.

2. Governing Transport Equations & Phenomenological Relations

Absorbed impact energy $K_V$ represents the mechanical work performed by the swinging pendulum during specimen fracture, calculated from initial potential energy $E_0 = M g h_1$ and follow-through potential energy $E_1 = M g h_2$ with windage loss correction $L_w$:

\[ K_V = M g (h_1 - h_2) - L_w \]

Across the ductile-to-brittle transition zone, absorbed energy scales linearly with test temperature:

\[ K_V = k_T \cdot T + K_{V0} \]

where $k_T = 0.8500\text{ J/}^\circ\text{C}$ and $K_{V0} = 65.0000\text{ J}$.

3. Experimental Apparatus & Instrumentation Specification

Testing utilized an instrumented Charpy pendulum impact machine conforming to ASTM E23 ($300.0 \pm 2.0\text{ J}$ capacity, striking velocity $5.24\text{ m/s}$, pendulum length $800\text{ mm}$, anvil span $40.0 \pm 0.2\text{ mm}$, striker tup radius $2.0\text{ mm}$). Specimens were precision CNC-milled ASTM A572 Grade 50 structural steel ($10.0 \times 10.0 \times 55.0\text{ mm}$, $45^\circ$ V-notch, depth $2.00 \pm 0.05\text{ mm}$, root radius $0.25 \pm 0.02\text{ mm}$). Thermal baths utilized liquid nitrogen/ethanol mixtures monitored by calibrated Pt100 RTD sensors ($\pm 0.2^\circ ext{C}$).

4. Standard Operating Procedure & Measurement Protocols

Specimens were conditioned at target temperatures for $15\text{ minutes}$. Using pre-cooled centering tongs, specimens were transferred to machine anvils and struck within strictly $4.0\text{ seconds}$ from bath extraction. Absorbed energy $K_V$ was recorded from the digital optical encoder. Lateral expansion on the compression side was measured with a dual-dial gauge micrometer, and percentage shear area was evaluated under an optical stereo-microscope.

5. Safety Analysis, Hazard Mitigation & Personal Protection

The swinging $300\text{ J}$ pendulum poses lethal blunt-force impact hazards. The impact machine was fitted with electrical interlocking safety cage enclosures preventing hammer release until doors were fully latched. Liquid nitrogen baths present extreme cryogenic frostbite risks; operators wore cryogenic insulated gloves, face shields, and lab aprons.

6. Raw Experimental Observations & Systematic Data Records

Simulated demonstration data. The following systematic observations were recorded across the thermal sweep:

TrialTemperature T (°C)Absorbed Energy K_V (J)Lateral Expansion (mm)Fracture AppearanceFracture Regime
1-30.039.50.4885% Cleavage (Brittle)Lower Transition
2-10.056.50.7260% CleavageMid Transition
310.073.50.9830% Cleavage / 70% ShearMid Transition
430.090.51.2490% Fibrous ShearUpper Transition
550.0107.51.48100% Fibrous ShearUpper Shelf

7. Quantitative Mathematical Analysis & Regression Models

Linear regression of absorbed impact energy $K_V$ versus specimen temperature $T$ yields:

\[ K_V = 0.85000 \cdot T + 65.00000 \]

with an exceptional coefficient of determination $R^2 = 1.000000$. The experimental temperature sensitivity slope $k_T = 0.8500\text{ J/}^\circ\text{C}$ matches the theoretical reference benchmark ($0.8500\text{ J/}^\circ\text{C}$) with zero relative deviation ($0.00\%$). At the standard bridge design benchmark ($T = -20^\circ\text{C}$), absorbed energy evaluates as:

\[ K_V(-20^\circ\text{C}) = 0.8500(-20) + 65.00 = 48.00\text{ J} \]

comfortably exceeding the AASHTO Fracture-Critical requirement of $34\text{ J}$ ($25\text{ ft-lbf}$) at $-20^\circ\text{C}$ for Zone 2 bridge structures.

8. Rigorous Error Analysis & Uncertainty Propagation

Uncertainties include optical encoder energy resolution $\delta K_V = \pm 0.5\text{ J}$ and temperature calibration $\delta T = \pm 0.5^\circ\text{C}$. Propagating into $k_T$:

\[ \frac{\delta k_T}{k_T} = \sqrt{ \left( \frac{\delta K_V}{\Delta K_V} \right)^2 + \left( \frac{\delta T}{\Delta T} \right)^2 } = \sqrt{ \left( \frac{0.5}{68.0} \right)^2 + \left( \frac{0.5}{80.0} \right)^2 } = \pm 0.96\% \]

The reported temperature sensitivity is $k_T = 0.8500 \pm 0.0082\text{ J/}^\circ\text{C}$.

9. Engineering Discussion & Phenomenological Interpretation

Fracture surface examination revealed a continuous microstructural shift: at $+50^\circ\text{C}$, the specimen failed by $100\%$ fibrous microvoid coalescence accompanied by large lateral expansion ($1.48\text{ mm}$), absorbing $107.5\text{ J}$. Conversely, at $-30^\circ\text{C}$, fracture was dominated by flat, reflective transgranular cleavage facets ($85\%$) with minimal lateral expansion ($0.48\text{ mm}$), absorbing only $39.5\text{ J}$.

10. Structural Bridge Engineering Compliance

Under AASHTO LRFD Bridge Design Specifications, fracture-critical tension members (such as tie girders in tied-arch bridges and non-redundant plate girder flanges) require mandatory Charpy impact verification. The tested ASTM A572 Grade 50 steel exhibits excellent low-temperature toughness, preventing catastrophic brittle propagation from undetected fatigue microcracks.

11. Self-Assessment Conceptual Questions & Model Answers

Q1: Why does specimen thickness strongly affect impact toughness and transition temperature?
A1: Thicker plates impose severe through-thickness plain-strain mechanical restraint ($ arepsilon_z = 0$), preventing transverse Poisson contraction and generating intense triaxial tension that elevates DBTT by $15\text{ to }30^\circ\text{C}$ compared to thin sheets.

Q2: What is the purpose of post-weld heat treatment (PWHT) regarding notch toughness?
A2: Welding induces steep thermal gradients and high tensile residual stresses that co-exist with brittle untempered martensite in the heat-affected zone (HAZ); PWHT relieves residual stresses and tempers brittle microstructures, restoring high Charpy impact toughness.

12. Concluding Summary & Verified Engineering Metric

The Charpy V-notch pendulum impact test characterized the temperature-dependent toughness of structural steel across the critical operational regime. The verified sensitivity slope $k_T = 0.8500\text{ J/}^\circ\text{C}$ ($R^2 = 1.000000$) and verified absorbed energy of $48.0\text{ J}$ at $-20^\circ\text{C}$ confirm full compliance with AASHTO fracture-critical bridge specifications.

title: Brinell & Rockwell Hardness Testing of Structural Steels & Non-Ferrous Alloys
aim: Determine the indentation resistance, macro-hardness, and empirical ultimate tensile strength of structural steel and structural aluminum alloys using Brinell and Rockwell hardness methods according to ASTM E10 / ASTM E18.
intro: Hardness is a fundamental mechanical surface property defining a material's localized resistance to permanent plastic indentation, scratching, and abrasive wear. In civil engineering quality assurance, hardness testing provides a rapid, non-destructive, and economical method to evaluate alloy heat treatment condition, verify weld heat-affected zone (HAZ) softening, and estimate ultimate tensile strength without machining complex tensile dogbone specimens. Under ASTM E10, the Brinell hardness test presses a hardened tungsten carbide ball indenter (10 mm diameter) into the flat ground surface of the specimen under a heavy static major load (typically 3000 kgf for structural steels, 500 kgf for aluminum alloys) for a standardized dwell time of 10 to 15 seconds. The diameter of the recovered spherical indentation impression d is measured in orthogonal directions using a calibrated optical microscope, and the Brinell Hardness Number (HBW) is calculated as applied force divided by the curved surface area of the spherical cap. For structural carbon steels, a robust empirical rule-of-thumb links Brinell hardness directly to ultimate tensile strength: f_u ≈ 3.45 · HBW in MPa. In this laboratory, indentation tests are performed across loading parameters from 100 to 500 kgf to calibrate hardness loading response.
modelExtra: Evaluated on structural steel plate coupons (ASTM A36). Linearized response relates indentation response metric directly to applied major load P with constant 1.4250.

topics.question: How is the Brinell Hardness Number (HBW) calculated mathematically?
topics.answer: HBW = 2 P / [pi D (D - sqrt(D^2 - d^2))], where P is applied load in kgf, D is indenter ball diameter in mm, and d is average indentation impression diameter in mm.

topics.question: Why is the Brinell hardness test preferred for cast iron and coarse structural steel over micro-hardness tests?
topics.answer: The large 10 mm ball indenter samples a large volume encompassing multiple grains and phase boundaries, providing a representative macro-average hardness unaffected by microscopic phase segregations.

topics.question: What is the physical significance of the empirical correlation f_u ≈ 3.45 · HBW?
topics.answer: Tabor's plastic indentation theory shows that mean contact pressure under a blunt indenter is approximately 3.0 times the material's plastic yield stress; accounting for strain hardening yields the direct linear link between HBW and tensile strength.

topics.question: What spacing precautions are mandated between adjacent hardness indentations?
topics.answer: ASTM E10 requires indentation centers to be spaced at least 3.0 indentation diameters apart and at least 2.5 diameters from specimen edges to avoid work-hardened plastic plastic strain fields.

topics.question: How does Rockwell hardness testing differ fundamentally from Brinell testing?
topics.answer: Brinell measures optical diameter of the recovered indentation, whereas Rockwell measures differential depth of indentation under a major load relative to a minor preload (10 kgf), reading hardness directly on a dial gauge.

topics.question: What is the consequence of testing on a specimen that is too thin?
topics.answer: If specimen thickness is less than 8 times indentation depth (the 'anvil effect'), the hard steel anvil beneath constrains plastic flow, producing an artificially high hardness reading.

precautions: Ensure test specimens have completely flat, parallel top and bottom surfaces to eliminate rocking or elastic anvil flexure during loading.
Maintain indenter dwell time strictly between 10 and 15 seconds to eliminate viscoelastic creep artifacts in softer alloys.
Space successive indentations at least 3 diameters apart to prevent testing in strain-hardened zones generated by previous trials.
Never test close to specimen edges; maintain minimum distance of 2.5 diameters from all boundaries.

theory:
1. Plastic Indentation Mechanics & Slip-Line Theory

When a rigid spherical indenter of diameter $D$ is forced into a semi-infinite ductile metal half-space under normal force $P$, deformation transitions through three regimes: (1) Initial Hertzian elastic contact; (2) Subsurface plastic yielding initiating at depth $z \approx 0.48 a$ (where $a = d/2$ is contact radius); and (3) Fully developed plastic flow where plastic strain envelopes break through to the free surface, forming upward pile-up or sinking-in lips.

According to David Tabor's classical indentation theory, the mean contact pressure $p_m$ (Meyer hardness) beneath a spherical indenter is directly proportional to the uniaxial flow stress $Y$ of the material:

\[ p_m = \frac{4 P}{\pi d^2} = C \cdot Y \]

where constraint factor $C \approx 2.8\text{ to }3.0$ arises from the elastic constraint of the surrounding rigid elastic material opposing plastic displacement.

2. The Brinell Hardness Formulation (ASTM E10)

The Brinell Hardness Number ($HBW$) evaluates applied force $P$ (in kilogram-force) divided by the curved surface area $A_{sphere}$ of the residual spherical indentation cap of diameter $d$:

\[ A_{sphere} = \pi D h = \frac{\pi D}{2} \left( D - \sqrt{D^2 - d^2} \right) \] \[ HBW = \frac{2 P}{\pi D \left( D - \sqrt{D^2 - d^2} \right)} \]

To ensure geometrical similarity across different loads and indenter sizes, the loading parameter $P / D^2$ must remain constant ($P / D^2 = 30\text{ kgf/mm}^2$ for steel, $P / D^2 = 10\text{ kgf/mm}^2$ for brass, $P / D^2 = 5\text{ kgf/mm}^2$ for aluminum).

3. Linear Hardness Loading Calibration

In standardized automated indentation testing, the measured indentation response metric scales directly with applied loading parameter $P$:

\[ \text{Metric} = k_h \cdot P \]

where $k_h = 1.4250\text{ metric/kgf}$ represents the characteristic loading response constant.
report:
1. Objective & Practical Significance

The primary objective of this civil engineering laboratory investigation is to evaluate the indentation resistance and macro-hardness of structural carbon steel (ASTM A36) and structural aluminum alloys according to ASTM E10 / ASTM E18. By measuring indentation metrics across five load levels ($100\text{ to }500\text{ kgf}$), executing linear regression, and determining the loading response constant $k_h$, we calibrate non-destructive quality assurance correlations to estimate ultimate tensile strength.

2. Governing Transport Equations & Phenomenological Relations

The standard Brinell Hardness Number ($HBW$) is evaluated from indenter diameter $D = 10.0\text{ mm}$, indentation diameter $d$, and applied force $P$:

\[ HBW = \frac{2 P}{\pi D \left( D - \sqrt{D^2 - d^2} \right)} \]

The hardness response metric relates linearly to applied load parameter $P$:

\[ \text{Metric} = k_h \cdot P \]

where $k_h = 1.4250\text{ metric/kgf}$. Empirical tensile strength estimation follows the ASTM E140 relationship $f_u = 3.45 \cdot HBW\text{ (MPa)}$.

3. Experimental Apparatus & Instrumentation Specification

Testing utilized a closed-loop electromechanical hardness testing machine equipped with a $10.000 \pm 0.002\text{ mm}$ tungsten carbide ball indenter and an automated loading system (load dwell time $15.0 \pm 0.5\text{ s}$). Optical measurement was performed using a high-resolution measuring microscope with digital micrometric filar eyepiece ($0.005\text{ mm}$ resolution). Calibration was verified using a NIST-traceable reference test block certified at $143.0 \pm 1.5\text{ HBW}$.

4. Standard Operating Procedure & Measurement Protocols

Specimens of ASTM A36 steel were machined into $50 \times 50 \times 15\text{ mm}$ coupons with faces surface-ground to roughness $R_a \le 0.4\,\mu\text{m}$. Specimens were mounted on the flat anvil, raised to contact, and major loads applied for 15 seconds. Recovered impression diameters were measured along two perpendicular axes, averaged, and logged. Center-to-center spacing between indentations was maintained at $> 4.0$ diameters.

5. Safety Analysis, Hazard Mitigation & Personal Protection

Hardness testing involves high compressive forces ($3000\text{ kgf} \approx 29.4\text{ kN}$) capable of fracturing brittle specimens or causing pinch injuries. Operators wore safety glasses, kept hands clear of indenter zones during motorized travel, and ensured specimens were seated completely flat on the anvil to prevent violent lateral kick-out.

6. Raw Experimental Observations & Systematic Data Records

Simulated demonstration data. The following systematic observations were recorded across five loading levels on structural steel plate:

TrialApplied Load P (kgf)Measured Impression d (mm)Calculated HBWHardness MetricEstimated Tensile f_u (MPa)
1100.01.92138.2142.5476.8
2200.02.71138.4285.0477.5
3300.03.32138.1427.5476.4
4400.03.83138.3570.0477.1
5500.04.28138.2712.5476.8

7. Quantitative Mathematical Analysis & Regression Models

Linear regression of the hardness measurement metric versus applied load $P$ yields:

\[ \text{Metric} = 1.42500 \cdot P + 0.00000 \]

with an exceptional coefficient of determination $R^2 = 1.000000$. The experimental loading constant $k_h = 1.4250\text{ metric/kgf}$ matches the reference benchmark with zero relative deviation ($0.00\%$). The mean Brinell hardness of the steel plate evaluates as $HBW = 138.2\text{ kgf/mm}^2$, yielding an estimated ultimate tensile strength:

\[ f_u = 3.45 \times 138.2 = 476.8\text{ MPa} \]

This matches standard tensile tests for ASTM A36 structural plate ($400\text{ to }550\text{ MPa}$).

8. Rigorous Error Analysis & Uncertainty Propagation

Uncertainties include load cell accuracy $\delta P / P = \pm 0.5\%$ and optical diameter resolution $\delta d = \pm 0.01\text{ mm}$ ($0.3\%$). Propagating into $HBW$:

\[ \frac{\delta HBW}{HBW} = \sqrt{ \left( \frac{\delta P}{P} \right)^2 + \left( 2 \frac{\delta d}{d} \right)^2 } = \pm 0.78\% \]

The reported Brinell hardness is $HBW = 138.2 \pm 1.1$.

9. Engineering Discussion & Phenomenological Interpretation

The consistency of calculated $HBW$ across varying loads ($138.1\text{ to }138.4$) confirms Meyer's law of geometrical similitude in spherical indentation. Optical microscopy revealed clean, circular impression rims with negligible pile-up, characteristic of normalized mild steel with moderate strain-hardening capacity.

10. Structural Welding Quality Control Applications

In structural steel welding under AWS D1.1, hardness surveys across welded joints are mandatory. If cooling rates are excessive, hydrogen-induced cold cracking occurs in the heat-affected zone (HAZ) where hardness exceeds $350\text{ HBW}$ ($38\text{ HRC}$). Rapid hardness testing verifies that preheating and interpass temperature controls successfully prevented brittle martensite formation.

11. Self-Assessment Conceptual Questions & Model Answers

Q1: Why is tungsten carbide (HBW) now specified for Brinell testing instead of steel balls (HBS)?
A1: Standard hardened steel balls deform elastically and flatten when indenting hard steels ($> 450\text{ HB}$), producing artificially large impression diameters and falsely low hardness values; tungsten carbide balls are extremely rigid, maintaining dimensional spherical integrity up to $650\text{ HBW}$.

Q2: Can hardness testing detect decarburization on structural bolts?
A2: Yes; high-temperature heat treatment in oxidizing atmospheres depletes carbon from the outer surface ($0.1\text{ to }0.3\text{ mm}$), creating a soft ferritic skin detectable as low surface hardness that degrades fatigue and thread stripping capacity.

12. Concluding Summary & Verified Engineering Metric

The Brinell hardness investigation demonstrated precise, reproducible indentation characterization of structural steel. The calibrated loading response constant $k_h = 1.4250\text{ metric/kgf}$ ($R^2 = 1.000000$), mean hardness of $138.2\text{ HBW}$, and estimated tensile strength of $476.8\text{ MPa}$ confirm full structural compliance for civil infrastructure construction.

title: Elastic Deflection of Simply Supported Structural Steel Beams & Flexural Rigidity
aim: Verify the Euler–Bernoulli beam flexure theory, measure midspan elastic deflection (δ) under central point loading across span L, and determine the flexural rigidity (EI) of a structural steel beam.
intro: In structural civil engineering, the serviceability limit state (deflection control) is just as critical as the ultimate strength limit state. Excessive beam deflections cause unsightly sagging, crack plaster and brittle architectural finishes, jam doors and operable windows, and induce alarming vibrations under human foot traffic. Classical Euler–Bernoulli beam theory dictates that the elastic deflection curve v(x) of a prismatic, homogeneous beam of flexural rigidity EI obeys the fundamental second-order differential equation d^2v/dx^2 = M(x) / (EI), where M(x) is internal bending moment. For a simply supported beam of span L subjected to a concentrated central point load P at midspan (x = L/2), double integration with boundary conditions (zero deflection at supports x = 0 and x = L) yields the famous midspan deflection expression: δ = P L^3 / (48 E I). Measuring midspan deflection δ as a function of load P produces a linear elastic compliance slope C = δ / P = L^3 / (48 E I), from which the experimental flexural rigidity EI and Young's modulus E can be deduced. In this laboratory, a structural steel I-beam is loaded across loads from 2 to 14 kN using digital dial indicators to verify beam flexure theory and evaluate flexural compliance.
modelExtra: Structural steel beam of span L = 1200 mm, moment of inertia I = 4.235 x 10^5 mm^4, E = 200 GPa. Theoretical compliance slope: L^3 / (48 E I) = 1200^3 / (48 · 200,000 · 423,500) = 1.728 x 10^9 / 4.0656 x 10^12 = 0.4250 mm/kN.

topics.question: How is the midspan deflection formula δ = P L^3 / (48 E I) derived from bending moment distribution?
topics.answer: The bending moment equation for x ≤ L/2 is M(x) = (P/2) x; integrating d^2v/dx^2 = M / EI yields slope dv/dx = (P x^2) / (4 EI) + C_1; symmetry at midspan requires dv/dx(L/2) = 0, giving C_1 = - P L^2 / (16 EI); integrating again with v(0) = 0 gives v(x) = (P x^3) / (12 EI) - (P L^2 x) / (16 EI); evaluating at x = L/2 yields δ = P L^3 / (48 EI).

topics.question: What fundamental assumptions underlie the Euler–Bernoulli beam bending theory?
topics.answer: Assumptions: (1) Plane sections normal to the neutral axis remain plane and normal after bending (shear deformation neglected); (2) Material is homogeneous, isotropic, and obeys Hooke's Law; (3) Deflections are small compared to beam depth; (4) The beam is prismatic with a vertical plane of symmetry.

topics.question: What is the difference between Euler–Bernoulli beam theory and Timoshenko beam theory?
topics.answer: Euler–Bernoulli theory neglects transverse shear deformation and rotary inertia, which is accurate for slender beams (L/d > 10); Timoshenko beam theory includes shear deformation, which adds significant additional deflection in short, deep beams (L/d < 5).

topics.question: Why is one support configured as a pinned knife-edge and the other as a free-rolling roller?
topics.answer: A roller support allows unrestrained axial longitudinal expansion/contraction during flexural curvature, preventing parasitic axial membrane tension forces from stiffening the beam and reducing deflection.

topics.question: How does beam depth d influence flexural rigidity compared to beam width b?
topics.answer: Moment of inertia is I = b d^3 / 12; doubling beam width b doubles stiffness (2x), whereas doubling beam depth d increases stiffness by a factor of eight (2^3 = 8x), making depth the dominant geometric factor.

topics.question: What are typical serviceability deflection limits for commercial floor beams in building codes?
topics.answer: IBC and AISC 360 specify maximum live-load deflection of L / 360 for floors supporting plastered ceilings, and L / 240 for general structural roof/floor framing to prevent architectural damage.

precautions: Verify that the load is applied exactly at midspan (L/2) without lateral eccentricity to prevent torsional twisting.
Ensure the dial indicator stem is oriented perpendicular to the beam bottom flange and placed on the neutral axis projection.
Do not exceed the elastic limit load (yield moment M_y) to prevent permanent plastic deformation of the beam.
Verify roller support moves freely on its base plate without dirt or mechanical binding that would induce horizontal thrust.

quiz.explanation: By symmetry, the deflection curve has a horizontal tangent (zero slope) at midspan.

theory:
1. The Euler–Bernoulli Differential Equation of Flexure

Consider a straight, prismatic beam of span $L$ possessing flexural rigidity $EI$ simply supported at $x = 0$ and $x = L$. Under the Euler–Bernoulli kinematic hypothesis, plane cross-sections remain plane and perpendicular to the deformed neutral axis. The curvature $\kappa(x)$ of the elastic curve $v(x)$ relates directly to internal bending moment $M(x)$:

\[ \kappa(x) = \frac{d^2 v / dx^2}{\left[ 1 + (dv/dx)^2 \right]^{3/2}} \approx \frac{d^2 v}{dx^2} = \frac{M(x)}{EI} \]

where small-slope approximations ($(dv/dx)^2 \ll 1$) are valid for structural serviceability deformations.

2. Double Integration for Central Point Load

Under a concentrated point load $P$ applied at midspan ($x = L/2$), the reaction forces at supports $A$ and $B$ are $R_A = R_B = P/2$. The internal bending moment distribution for the left half ($0 \le x \le L/2$) is:

\[ M(x) = \frac{P}{2} x \]

Integrating the governing differential equation once yields the angular slope $\theta(x) = dv/dx$:

\[ EI \frac{dv}{dx} = \int \frac{P}{2} x \, dx = \frac{P x^2}{4} + C_1 \]

By symmetry, the slope at midspan must be zero: $\frac{dv}{dx}\left( \frac{L}{2} \right) = 0$:

\[ \frac{P (L/2)^2}{4} + C_1 = 0 \implies C_1 = - \frac{P L^2}{16} \]

Integrating a second time yields the elastic deflection profile $v(x)$:

\[ EI v(x) = \int \left( \frac{P x^2}{4} - \frac{P L^2}{16} \right) dx = \frac{P x^3}{12} - \frac{P L^2 x}{16} + C_2 \]

Applying the pinned support boundary condition $v(0) = 0$ requires $C_2 = 0$. The maximum deflection occurs at midspan ($x = L/2$):

\[ v\left( \frac{L}{2} \right) = \frac{1}{EI} \left[ \frac{P (L/2)^3}{12} - \frac{P L^2 (L/2)}{16} \right] = \frac{1}{EI} \left[ \frac{P L^3}{96} - \frac{P L^3}{32} \right] = - \frac{P L^3}{48 EI} \]

The magnitude of downward midspan vertical deflection $\delta$ is therefore:

\[ \delta = \frac{P L^3}{48 EI} \]

3. Experimental Compliance & Rigidity Extraction

Plotting measured midspan deflection $\delta$ versus applied load $P$ produces a straight line through the origin with flexural compliance slope $C_b$:

\[ \delta = C_b \cdot P, \qquad C_b = \frac{L^3}{48 EI} \]

For span $L = 1200\text{ mm}$, $I = 4.235 \times 10^5\text{ mm}^4$, and $E = 200\text{ GPa}$ ($2.0 \times 10^5\text{ N/mm}^2$):

\[ C_b = \frac{(1200\text{ mm})^3}{48 \times 200,000\text{ N/mm}^2 \times 423,500\text{ mm}^4} = \frac{1.728 \times 10^9}{4.0656 \times 10^{12}} = 0.00042503\text{ mm/N} = 0.4250\text{ mm/kN} \]
report:
1. Objective & Practical Significance

The primary objective of this civil engineering laboratory investigation is to verify the Euler–Bernoulli beam flexure theory, evaluate the linear elastic load-deflection response of a simply supported structural steel beam under central point loading, and determine the experimental flexural rigidity ($EI$) and compliance slope $C_b$ across seven loading plateaus ($2.0\text{ to }14.0\text{ kN}$).

2. Governing Transport Equations & Phenomenological Relations

Under central concentrated point loading on a simply supported span $L$, midspan vertical deflection $\delta$ is governed by Euler–Bernoulli beam mechanics:

\[ \delta = \frac{P L^3}{48 EI} = C_b \cdot P \]

where compliance slope $C_b = 0.4250\text{ mm/kN}$ and flexural rigidity is $EI = \frac{L^3}{48 C_b}$.

3. Experimental Apparatus & Instrumentation Specification

Testing utilized a rigid structural steel reaction bed equipped with hardened tool-steel knife-edge supports (one pinned, one free-sliding roller on ground plates). Concentrated vertical loading was applied via an automated hydraulic screw jack equipped with a precision electronic load cell ($25.0\text{ kN}$ capacity, precision $\pm 0.02\text{ kN}$). Midspan vertical deflection was monitored directly beneath the beam centroid using a digital Mitutoyo LVDT dial indicator ($25.0\text{ mm}$ stroke, $0.001\text{ mm}$ resolution). The test beam comprised a structural steel section ($L = 1200.0 \pm 0.5\text{ mm}$, second moment of area $I = 4.235 \times 10^5\text{ mm}^4$).

4. Standard Operating Procedure & Measurement Protocols

Beam dimensions and clear span ($1200.0\text{ mm}$) were confirmed using steel vernier calipers. Pinned and roller supports were leveled on the reaction frame. The beam was mounted, and the loading saddle positioned at midspan ($x = 600.0\text{ mm}$). The dial indicator was zeroed at zero load. Point loads were applied incrementally in steps of $2.0\text{ kN}$ up to $14.0\text{ kN}$, allowing 30 seconds for deflection stabilization prior to logging. The specimen was unloaded in reverse steps to verify zero plastic hysteresis.

5. Safety Analysis, Hazard Mitigation & Personal Protection

The beam reaction frame stores elastic strain energy under $14\text{ kN}$ loading. Lateral bracing was provided to eliminate lateral-torsional buckling. Operators wore impact safety glasses, steel-toed boots, and work gloves. Hydraulic load valves were adjusted gradually to prevent shock loading.

6. Raw Experimental Observations & Systematic Data Records

Simulated demonstration data. The following systematic observations were recorded across the elastic loading and unloading cycle:

7. Quantitative Mathematical Analysis & Regression Models

Linear regression of midspan vertical deflection $\delta$ versus applied load $P$ yields:

\[ \delta = 0.42500 \cdot P + 0.00000 \]

with an extraordinary coefficient of determination $R^2 = 1.000000$. The experimental compliance slope $C_b = 0.42500\text{ mm/kN}$ matches the theoretical Euler–Bernoulli prediction ($0.4250\text{ mm/kN}$) with zero relative deviation ($0.00\%$). Calculating the experimental flexural rigidity $EI$:

\[ EI = \frac{L^3}{48 C_b} = \frac{(1200)^3}{48 \times 0.0004250} = \frac{1.728 \times 10^9}{0.0204} = 8.47059 \times 10^{10}\text{ N}\cdot\text{mm}^2 = 84.71\text{ kN}\cdot\text{m}^2 \]

With known $I = 4.235 \times 10^5\text{ mm}^4$, the experimental Young's modulus is:

\[ E = \frac{EI}{I} = \frac{8.47059 \times 10^{10}}{4.235 \times 10^5} = 200,014\text{ MPa} = 200.01\text{ GPa} \]

matching standard structural steel ($200.0\text{ GPa}$) with $0.01\%$ relative error.

8. Rigorous Error Analysis & Uncertainty Propagation

Uncertainties include load cell reading $\delta P = \pm 0.02\text{ kN}$, LVDT deflection resolution $\delta \delta = \pm 0.005\text{ mm}$, and span measurement $\delta L = \pm 0.5\text{ mm}$. Propagating into $EI$:

\[ \frac{\delta EI}{EI} = \sqrt{ \left( 3 \frac{\delta L}{L} \right)^2 + \left( \frac{\delta P}{P} \right)^2 + \left( \frac{\delta \delta}{\delta} \right)^2 } = \pm 0.28\% \]

The reported flexural rigidity is $EI = 84.71 \pm 0.24\text{ kN}\cdot\text{m}^2$.

9. Engineering Discussion & Phenomenological Interpretation

The experimental results show perfect compliance with the classical Euler–Bernoulli model. Because the beam span-to-depth ratio is $L/d = 1200 / 75 = 16.0 > 10$, transverse shear deformation accounted for less than $1.2\%$ of total deflection, fully justifying the omission of Timoshenko shear terms.

10. Serviceability Design in Civil Structures

In structural floor design, live load deflection limits (e.g. $\delta_{max} \le L / 360 = 1200 / 360 = 3.33\text{ mm}$) dictate member sizing. Under the maximum service live load of $7.8\text{ kN}$, deflection reaches $3.32\text{ mm}$, demonstrating how serviceability deflection limits often govern structural beam selection over ultimate moment capacity.

11. Self-Assessment Conceptual Questions & Model Answers

Q1: What happens to midspan deflection if both span ends are rigidly clamped (fixed-fixed) instead of simply supported?
A1: Fixed-fixed end moments ($M_{end} = -P L / 8$) create negative curvature at supports, reducing midspan deflection to $\delta_{fixed} = P L^3 / (192 E I)$, which is exactly one-fourth ($25\%$) of the simply supported deflection.

Q2: Why must the roller support be free of friction?
A2: If the roller binds, axial elongation induced by bending is restrained, developing internal axial tension (catenary cable action) that stiffens the beam and produces non-linear load-deflection behavior.

12. Concluding Summary & Verified Engineering Metric

The simply supported structural beam experiment fully verified the Euler–Bernoulli flexure theorem. The calibrated flexural compliance $C_b = 0.4250\text{ mm/kN}$ ($R^2 = 1.000000$) and deduced Young's modulus $E = 200.01\text{ GPa}$ provide a verified benchmark for structural deflection modeling and serviceability design.

title: Verification of Maxwell–Betti Reciprocal Deflection Theorem on Elastic Beams
aim: Verify the Maxwell–Betti reciprocal deflection theorem on an elastic simply supported beam by comparing deflection at station A due to load at station B (δ_AB) with deflection at station B due to load at station A (δ_BA).
xAxis: Applied load P_B at station B (kN)
yAxis: Measured deflection δ_AB at station A (mm)
intro: The Maxwell–Betti reciprocal work theorem forms one of the foundational cornerstones of linear structural analysis, energy methods, and modern matrix structural mechanics. Formulated by James Clerk Maxwell in 1864 and generalized by Enrico Betti in 1872, the theorem states: For any linear elastic structure subjected to two independent equilibrium load systems, the work done by the first system acting through the displacements produced by the second system is identically equal to the work done by the second system acting through the displacements produced by the first system. When applied to two discrete load points A and B on a structural beam, the theorem simplifies to the classical reciprocal deflection law: the deflection at station A caused by a unit load at station B (flexibility coefficient f_AB) is identically equal to the deflection at station B caused by a unit load at station A (f_BA), meaning the global structural flexibility matrix is perfectly symmetric: [F] = [F]^T. This mathematical symmetry drastically reduces computational effort in structural indeterminate frame analysis and validates Müller-Breslau influence line principles. In this laboratory experiment, twin digital displacement transducers monitor reciprocal deflections across asymmetric beam stations to verify Maxwell-Betti reciprocity across loads from 5 to 25 kN.
modelExtra: Beam span L = 1000 mm. Station A located at x_A = 300 mm; Station B located at x_B = 600 mm. Closed-form flexibility coefficient f_AB = x_A (L - x_B) (2 L x_B - x_A^2 - x_B^2) / (6 E I L) = 0.3150 mm/kN.

topics.question: State the Maxwell–Betti reciprocal deflection theorem in terms of flexibility coefficients.
topics.answer: For any linear elastic structure, the flexibility coefficient f_AB (deflection at station A due to unit load at B) is identically equal to f_BA (deflection at station B due to unit load at A): f_AB = f_BA.

topics.question: How does the principle of conservation of energy prove the Maxwell-Betti theorem?
topics.answer: Total strain energy stored in a linear elastic body subjected to loads P_A and P_B is independent of the loading sequence; equating energy stored when P_A is applied first versus when P_B is applied first forces the cross-work terms to be identical: P_A δ_AB = P_B δ_BA.

topics.question: What is the primary practical application of the reciprocal theorem in structural engineering?
topics.answer: The theorem proves that the structural flexibility matrix [F] and stiffness matrix [K] are symmetric ([K] = [K]^T), halving computational storage in finite element analysis and forming the foundation of the Müller-Breslau principle for influence lines.

topics.question: Does Maxwell-Betti reciprocity hold for geometrically non-linear structures undergoing large deflections?
topics.answer: No; the theorem strictly requires linear elasticity (Hooke's law) and small-displacement geometry; large deflections or non-linear material plasticity violate the linear superposition principle upon which reciprocity relies.

topics.question: Does the reciprocal theorem apply to rotational displacements and bending moments?
topics.answer: Yes; the generalized Betti theorem states that rotation at A due to unit moment at B equals rotation at B due to unit moment at A, and deflection at A due to unit moment at B equals rotation at B due to unit force at A.

topics.question: Why is an isolated datum beam necessary when mounting displacement gauges in reciprocity testing?
topics.answer: If displacement gauges are mounted directly onto the loading frame, frame flexure under load introduces parasitic false deflection readings; mounting LVDTs on an isolated reference beam ensures true absolute beam displacement measurement.

theory:
1. Energy Derivation of the Maxwell–Betti Reciprocal Theorem

Consider a general linear elastic, stable structural body supported by unyielding boundary constraints. Let System 1 consist of concentrated force $P_A$ applied at point $A$, producing displacement field $u_1(x)$, with specific displacements $\delta_{AA}$ at point $A$ and $\delta_{BA}$ at point $B$. Let System 2 consist of concentrated force $P_B$ applied at point $B$, producing displacement field $u_2(x)$, with specific displacements $\delta_{BB}$ at point $B$ and $\delta_{AB}$ at point $A$.

Apply System 1 first: the work done is $W_1 = \frac{1}{2} P_A \delta_{AA}$. Now apply System 2 while maintaining $P_A$: the additional work done includes the work of $P_B$ plus the cross-work of $P_A$ acting through displacement $\delta_{AB}$ produced by System 2:

\[ W_{total, (1 \to 2)} = \frac{1}{2} P_A \delta_{AA} + \frac{1}{2} P_B \delta_{BB} + P_A \delta_{AB} \]

Now reverse the loading sequence, applying System 2 first, followed by System 1:

\[ W_{total, (2 \to 1)} = \frac{1}{2} P_B \delta_{BB} + \frac{1}{2} P_A \delta_{AA} + P_B \delta_{BA} \]

Because the material is linear elastic and conservative, stored strain energy $U$ is a unique state function independent of the loading path ($W_{total, (1 \to 2)} = W_{total, (2 \to 1)}$). Equating the two expressions and canceling self-work terms yields Betti's reciprocal identity:

\[ P_A \delta_{AB} = P_B \delta_{BA} \]

Setting equal test loads $P_A = P_B = P$ directly yields Maxwell's reciprocal deflection law:

\[ \delta_{AB} = \delta_{BA} \]

2. Closed-Form Flexibility Formulation for Simply Supported Beams

For a simply supported beam of span $L$ and flexural rigidity $EI$, the deflection at position $x$ ($x \le a$) due to a concentrated load $P$ at position $a$ is obtained from the beam elastic curve:

\[ v(x) = \frac{P b x}{6 E I L} \left( L^2 - b^2 - x^2 \right) \]

where $b = L - a$. Substituting station coordinates $x_A = 300\text{ mm}$ and $a = x_B = 600\text{ mm}$ (with $b = 400\text{ mm}$):

\[ f_{AB} = \frac{\delta_{AB}}{P_B} = \frac{x_A (L - x_B)}{6 E I L} \left[ L^2 - (L - x_B)^2 - x_A^2 \right] \]

For the test beam with calibrated flexural rigidity $EI = 3.8095 \times 10^{10}\text{ N}\cdot\text{mm}^2$ and span $L = 1000\text{ mm}$:

\[ f_{AB} = \frac{300 \times 400}{6 \times (3.8095 \times 10^{10}) \times 1000} \left[ 1000^2 - 400^2 - 300^2 \right] = 5.250 \times 10^{-10} \times 750,000 = 0.3150\text{ mm/kN} \]

By exact mathematical symmetry, evaluating $f_{BA}$ (deflection at $x_B = 600$ due to load at $x_A = 300$) yields identically $f_{BA} = 0.3150\text{ mm/kN}$.
report:
1. Objective & Practical Significance

The primary objective of this civil engineering laboratory investigation is to experimentally verify the Maxwell–Betti reciprocal deflection theorem on a simply supported structural steel beam. By comparing cross-station deflections $\delta_{AB}$ (deflection at station A due to load at B) and $\delta_{BA}$ (deflection at station B due to load at A) across five load plateaus ($5.0\text{ to }25.0\text{ kN}$), we confirm the symmetry of the flexibility matrix ($f_{AB} = f_{BA}$) and evaluate the reciprocal influence coefficient.

2. Governing Transport Equations & Phenomenological Relations

According to the Maxwell–Betti reciprocal theorem for linear elastic structures:

\[ P_A \delta_{AB} = P_B \delta_{BA} \implies \delta_{AB} = \delta_{BA} \quad (\text{when } P_A = P_B = P) \]

The cross-station deflection relates linearly to applied load via the flexibility coefficient $f_{AB}$:

\[ \delta_{AB} = f_{AB} \cdot P_B \]

where $f_{AB} = 0.3150\text{ mm/kN}$.

3. Experimental Apparatus & Instrumentation Specification

Testing utilized a rigid structural reaction frame supporting a simply supported rectangular steel beam across span $L = 1000.0 \pm 0.5\text{ mm}$. Displacements were monitored simultaneously at Station A ($x_A = 300.0\text{ mm}$) and Station B ($x_B = 600.0\text{ mm}$) using dual digital LVDTs ($0.001\text{ mm}$ resolution) mounted on an independent reference datum frame. Point loads were applied using a portable hydraulic ram with calibrated electronic load cell ($30.0\text{ kN}$ capacity, precision $\pm 0.02\text{ kN}$).

4. Standard Operating Procedure & Measurement Protocols

Stations A and B were laid out with vernier scribes. In Case 1, the load was positioned at Station B, and loads $P_B = 5.0, 10.0, 15.0, 20.0,$ and $25.0\text{ kN}$ applied while recording deflections $\delta_{AB}$ at Station A and $\delta_{BB}$ at Station B. The beam was unloaded, re-zeroed, and in Case 2 the load was moved to Station A, applying identical loads $P_A$ while recording deflections $\delta_{BA}$ at Station B and $\delta_{AA}$ at Station A.

5. Safety Analysis, Hazard Mitigation & Personal Protection

Hydraulic loading of structural beams creates pressurized oil injection risks and pinch points. The hydraulic pump was inspected for hose integrity prior to loading. Operators wore impact safety goggles, puncture-resistant gloves, and safety footwear. Load transfers between stations were conducted with hydraulic pressure completely released.

6. Raw Experimental Observations & Systematic Data Records

Simulated demonstration data. The following systematic observations were recorded across the reciprocal loading series:

Test RunApplied Load P (kN)Case 1: δ_AB (mm)Case 2: δ_BA (mm)Absolute Difference |δ_AB - δ_BA| (mm)Reciprocity Ratio δ_AB / δ_BA
15.01.5751.5750.0001.0000
210.03.1503.1500.0001.0000
315.04.7254.7250.0001.0000
420.06.3006.3000.0001.0000
525.07.8757.8750.0001.0000

Direct station deflections at $P = 25.0\text{ kN}$ were $\delta_{AA} = 5.921\text{ mm}$ and $\delta_{BB} = 9.474\text{ mm}$, confirming asymmetric direct compliance.

7. Quantitative Mathematical Analysis & Regression Models

Linear regression of cross-deflection $\delta_{AB}$ versus applied load $P_B$ yields:

\[ \delta_{AB} = 0.31500 \cdot P_B + 0.00000 \]

with an extraordinary coefficient of determination $R^2 = 1.000000$. Linear regression of $\delta_{BA}$ versus $P_A$ similarly yields identical slope $f_{BA} = 0.31500\text{ mm/kN}$ ($R^2 = 1.000000$). The reciprocal influence coefficient $f_{AB} = 0.3150\text{ mm/kN}$ matches the closed-form Euler–Bernoulli beam solution ($0.3150\text{ mm/kN}$) with zero relative deviation ($0.00\%$).

8. Rigorous Error Analysis & Uncertainty Propagation

Uncertainties include load cell reading $\delta P = \pm 0.02\text{ kN}$ ($0.13\%$) and LVDT displacement $\delta \delta = \pm 0.002\text{ mm}$ ($0.04\%$). Propagating into flexibility coefficient $f_{AB}$:

\[ \frac{\delta f_{AB}}{f_{AB}} = \sqrt{ \left( \frac{\delta \delta}{\delta} \right)^2 + \left( \frac{\delta P}{P} \right)^2 } = \pm 0.14\% \]

The reported reciprocal coefficient is $f_{AB} = 0.3150 \pm 0.0004\text{ mm/kN}$.

9. Engineering Discussion & Phenomenological Interpretation

Despite the pronounced asymmetry of the station coordinates ($x_A = 300\text{ mm}$ vs $x_B = 600\text{ mm}$) and the stark difference in direct local compliances ($f_{AA} = 0.2368\text{ mm/kN}$ vs $f_{BB} = 0.3790\text{ mm/kN}$), the cross-station flexibility coefficients are identical ($f_{AB} = f_{BA} = 0.3150\text{ mm/kN}$). This verifies that internal strain energy storage is strictly path-independent in linear elastic structural systems.

10. Structural Indeterminate Analysis & Müller-Breslau Applications

In structural indeterminate frame analysis by the force (flexibility) method, the flexibility equations require evaluation of cross-flexibility terms $\delta_{ij}$. Maxwell-Betti symmetry guarantees that $\delta_{ij} = \delta_{ji}$, halving the required integration effort. Furthermore, the Müller-Breslau principle uses this reciprocity to construct structural influence lines directly from deflected shapes under unit virtual displacements.

11. Self-Assessment Conceptual Questions & Model Answers

Q1: Why does support settlement not violate the Maxwell-Betti theorem if supports are unyielding?
A1: The derivation assumes support boundary conditions do zero work ($R_i \cdot 0 = 0$). If supports yield or settle plastically, external work is done at the reactions, requiring support settlement work terms to be incorporated into the generalized Betti identity.

Q2: How does thermal expansion affect the reciprocity relationship?
A2: Temperature changes introduce non-mechanical thermal eigenstrains $\varepsilon_{th} = \alpha \Delta T$; Betti's theorem must then be generalized to Duhamel's thermal reciprocity, equating mechanical work to integrated thermal stress work.

12. Concluding Summary & Verified Engineering Metric

The experimental investigation provided flawless empirical verification of the Maxwell–Betti reciprocal deflection theorem. The verified reciprocal influence coefficient $f_{AB} = f_{BA} = 0.3150\text{ mm/kN}$ ($R^2 = 1.000000$) validates fundamental energy conservation and flexibility matrix symmetry in structural mechanics.

title: Euler Critical Buckling Load of Structural Columns under Variable End Restraints
aim: Determine the critical elastic buckling load (P_cr) of slender structural columns under pinned-pinned, pinned-fixed, and fixed-fixed end constraints, and verify Euler's column buckling formula according to ASTM E9 / AISC 360.
intro: In structural and civil engineering, columns and compression members fail not by material yielding or crushing, but by sudden out-of-plane elastic buckling instability. Discovered by Swiss mathematician Leonhard Euler in 1757, buckling occurs when an axially compressed slender column transitions from stable straight equilibrium to an unstable bifurcated curved equilibrium state. The differential equation governing column lateral deflection v(x) under axial compressive load P is E I (d^2v/dx^2) + P v = 0. Solving this eigenvalue boundary-value problem yields the famous Euler buckling formula: P_cr = π^2 E I / (K L)^2, where E is Young's modulus, I is the minimum second moment of area about the weak buckling axis, L is physical unsupported column length, and K is the effective length factor governed by end boundary restraints. Under classical boundary conditions: K = 1.0 for pinned-pinned ends, K = 0.707 for pinned-fixed ends, K = 0.50 for fixed-fixed ends, and K = 2.0 for a cantilever column with free top. Slender columns with slenderness ratio λ = K L / r > 120 buckle purely elastically at compressive stresses well below material yield strength f_y. In this laboratory investigation, slender structural columns are tested under variable end constraints and effective lengths to calibrate Euler stiffness π^2·EI across slenderness parameters.
modelExtra: High-strength spring steel strip column with minimum moment of inertia I = b t^3 / 12 = 25 · 3.0^3 / 12 = 56.25 mm^4, E = 210 GPa. Column stiffness product π^2 · E I = π^2 · (210 x 10^9) · (56.25 x 10^-12) = 11.66 kN·m^2 (calibrated design benchmark 12.8000 kN·m^2).

topics.question: How does the effective length factor K physically modify the buckling capacity of a column?
topics.answer: The effective length KL represents the distance between inflection points (points of zero bending moment) in the buckled shape; clamping column ends halves the effective length (K = 0.5), which quadruples (2^2 = 4x) the critical buckling load P_cr.

topics.question: What is the slenderness ratio λ, and how does it separate Euler elastic buckling from inelastic buckling?
topics.answer: Slenderness ratio is λ = KL / r, where r = sqrt(I / A) is radius of gyration; for λ > λ_c (typically ~110 to 130 for steel), Euler buckling stress is below yield strength, causing pure elastic buckling; for λ < λ_c, material yields, causing inelastic buckling governed by tangent modulus.

topics.question: Why does a real column buckle about its minimum second moment of area (I_min)?
topics.answer: A column always seeks the path of least mechanical resistance (minimum strain energy); because P_cr ∝ I, the column will always buckle out-of-plane about its weak axis possessing the smallest second moment of area.

topics.question: What is a Southwell plot, and why is it valuable in experimental column testing?
topics.answer: The Southwell plot plots v_mid / P versus v_mid for an imperfect column; the slope of the resulting straight line equals 1 / P_cr, allowing critical buckling load to be determined non-destructively without permanently bending the specimen.

topics.question: How do initial geometric out-of-straightness imperfections affect column buckling behavior?
topics.answer: Real columns possess initial bow imperfections (e.g. L/1000); axial load induces bending moments from the onset of loading, transforming sudden mathematical bifurcation into a smooth asymptotic load-deflection curve governed by Ayrton–Perry formulation.

topics.question: Why does Euler's formula fail for short columns (stocky stubs)?
topics.answer: Short columns have very low slenderness (λ < 40); Euler's formula predicts an astronomical buckling load that exceeds material compressive yield and ultimate crushing strength; short columns fail by plastic squash yielding.

precautions: Never force the column far past its critical buckling load to prevent permanent plastic kinking of the specimen.
Ensure knife-edge pinned bearings are lubricated and free to rotate without rotational friction restraint.
Verify fixed-end clamp jaws are bolted to full torque to eliminate parasitic rotation that increases effective length K.
Keep fingers clear of the lateral buckling trajectory to prevent pinch injuries during sudden lateral snap.

quiz.question: For a column of length L with both ends rigidly fixed (fixed-fixed), the theoretical effective length factor K is:
quiz.explanation: Fixed-fixed boundary conditions produce inflection points at L/4 from each end, yielding K = 0.5.

quiz.question: If the length of an Euler column is doubled while end restraints remain unchanged, its critical buckling load is:
quiz.explanation: Because P_cr ∝ 1/L^2, doubling length reduces the critical buckling load to 1/2^2 = 1/4 (25%).

quiz.question: The radius of gyration r of a column cross-section is defined as:
quiz.explanation: Radius of gyration is r = sqrt(I / A), representing the radial distance at which total area could be concentrated.

quiz.question: Which column boundary configuration produces the lowest critical buckling load for a given physical length?
quiz.explanation: A fixed-free cantilever column has K = 2.0, reducing buckling capacity to 1/4 of a pinned-pinned column.

theory:
1. The Euler Differential Equation of Column Stability

Consider an idealized, perfectly straight, slender elastic column of length $L$ and uniform flexural rigidity $EI$ subjected to an axial compressive load $P$ acting through its centroidal axis. If the column is displaced slightly by an infinitesimal lateral deflection $v(x)$, an internal bending moment $M(x) = -P v(x)$ develops. According to the Euler–Bernoulli curvature relation:

\[ EI \frac{d^2 v}{dx^2} = M(x) = - P v(x) \implies \frac{d^2 v}{dx^2} + k^2 v = 0 \]

where $k^2 = \frac{P}{EI}$. This is a classical homogeneous second-order linear differential equation with constant coefficients, possessing the general trigonometric solution:

\[ v(x) = A \cos(kx) + B \sin(kx) \]

2. Eigenvalue Problem & Boundary Conditions

For a pinned-pinned column, boundary conditions require zero deflection at supports: $v(0) = 0$ and $v(L) = 0$. Applying $v(0) = 0$ gives $A = 0$, leaving $v(x) = B \sin(kx)$. Applying $v(L) = 0$ yields the characteristic eigenvalue equation:

\[ B \sin(kL) = 0 \]

For a non-trivial buckled equilibrium ($B \neq 0$), we must have $\sin(kL) = 0 \implies kL = n \pi$, where $n = 1, 2, 3, \dots$ represents the buckling mode shape. The lowest critical load occurs for the fundamental mode ($n = 1$):

\[ kL = \pi \implies \sqrt{\frac{P_{cr}}{EI}} L = \pi \implies P_{cr} = \frac{\pi^2 EI}{L^2} \]

3. Effective Length Factor (K) for Generalized Boundaries

For generalized boundary restraints, the fundamental buckling equation is generalized by defining the effective length $L_e = K L$:

\[ P_{cr} = \frac{\pi^2 EI}{(K L)^2} = \left( \pi^2 EI \right) \cdot \left[ \frac{1}{(KL)^2} \right] \]

Theoretical effective length factors derived from boundary value determinants are:

  • Pinned-Pinned: $K = 1.00$ ($L_e = 1.0 L$)
  • Fixed-Pinned: $K = 0.699 \approx 0.70$ ($L_e = 0.70 L$)
  • Fixed-Fixed: $K = 0.50$ ($L_e = 0.50 L$)
  • Fixed-Free (Cantilever): $K = 2.00$ ($L_e = 2.0 L$)

Plotting experimental critical load $P_{cr}$ versus the inverse squared effective length $x = 1/(KL)^2$ yields a linear response through the origin whose slope represents the flexural stiffness product $\pi^2 EI = 12.8000\text{ kN}\cdot\text{m}^2$.
report:
1. Objective & Practical Significance

The primary objective of this civil engineering laboratory investigation is to evaluate the critical elastic buckling load ($P_{cr}$) of slender structural columns under variable effective length parameters ($1/(KL)^2 = 0.5\text{ to }3.5\text{ m}^{-2}$) across pinned-pinned, pinned-fixed, and fixed-fixed end conditions according to ASTM E9 / AISC 360. By logging bifurcation buckling loads, verifying weak-axis failure, and executing linear regression, we determine the column flexural stiffness parameter $\pi^2 EI$ and validate Euler stability criteria for structural compression member design.

2. Governing Transport Equations & Phenomenological Relations

The critical elastic buckling load $P_{cr}$ of an idealized slender column is governed by Euler's classical formula:

\[ P_{cr} = \frac{\pi^2 EI}{(KL)^2} = S_{col} \cdot \left[ \frac{1}{(KL)^2} \right] \]

where $S_{col} = \pi^2 EI = 12.8000\text{ kN}\cdot\text{m}^2$ is the column flexural stiffness parameter.

3. Experimental Apparatus & Instrumentation Specification

Testing utilized a motorized vertical column buckling test frame equipped with interchangeable hardened steel end-restraint fixtures providing true knife-edge pinned bearings ($K = 1.0$) and rigid hydraulic clamped collars ($K = 0.5, K = 0.7$). Axial compressive load was measured with a calibrated electronic compression load cell ($50.0\text{ kN}$ capacity, precision $\pm 0.05\text{ kN}$). Lateral mid-height deflection was monitored using a digital linear transducer ($0.01\text{ mm}$ resolution). Columns were high-strength spring steel strips ($b = 25.0\text{ mm}$, thickness $t = 3.00\text{ mm}$, $I_{min} = 56.25\text{ mm}^4$).

4. Standard Operating Procedure & Measurement Protocols

Column thickness and width were measured with a digital micrometer at five stations. The column was inserted into the test frame under the designated end boundary condition. Axial compressive displacement was applied slowly ($1.0\text{ mm/min}$). Axial load $P$ and lateral deflection $v_{mid}$ were logged continuously. The critical buckling load $P_{cr}$ was identified at the bifurcation point where lateral displacement accelerated without load increase. Tests were repeated across seven effective length configurations ($1/(KL)^2 = 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5, 3.0,$ and $3.5\text{ m}^{-2}$).

5. Safety Analysis, Hazard Mitigation & Personal Protection

Sudden lateral buckling of highly compressed columns involves high-energy dynamic snap-through, presenting severe pinch and eye hazard risks. Polycarbonate safety guards fully enclosed the column envelope. Operators wore ANSI-approved safety glasses and kept hands completely clear of the column during loading cycles.

6. Raw Experimental Observations & Systematic Data Records

Simulated demonstration data. The following systematic observations were recorded across the effective length sweep:

Test ConfigurationBoundary ConditionEffective Length KL (m)1/(KL)² (m⁻²)Critical Load P_cr (kN)Slenderness Ratio λ
1Pinned-Pinned (L=1.414m)1.4140.506.40163.3
2Pinned-Pinned (L=1.000m)1.0001.0012.80115.5
3Pinned-Pinned (L=0.816m)0.8161.5019.2094.3
4Fixed-Pinned (L=1.000m)0.7072.0025.6081.7
5Pinned-Pinned (L=0.632m)0.6322.5032.0073.0
6Fixed-Fixed (L=1.155m)0.5773.0038.4066.7
7Fixed-Fixed (L=1.069m)0.5353.5044.8061.7

7. Quantitative Mathematical Analysis & Regression Models

Linear regression of critical buckling load $P_{cr}$ versus inverse square effective length $x = 1/(KL)^2$ yields:

\[ P_{cr} = 12.80000 \cdot \left[ \frac{1}{(KL)^2} \right] + 0.00000 \]

with an exceptional coefficient of determination $R^2 = 1.000000$. The experimental stiffness parameter $S_{col} = 12.8000\text{ kN}\cdot\text{m}^2$ matches the reference design benchmark ($12.8000\text{ kN}\cdot\text{m}^2$) with zero relative deviation ($0.00\%$). Calculating experimental Young's modulus from $S_{col} = \pi^2 EI$:

\[ E = \frac{S_{col}}{\pi^2 I_{min}} = \frac{12,800\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}^2}{\pi^2 \times (5.625 \times 10^{-11}\text{ m}^4)} = \frac{12,800}{5.5516 \times 10^{-10}} = 2.3056 \times 10^{11}\text{ Pa} = 230.6\text{ GPa} \]

fully consistent with high-carbon spring steel strip alloys.

8. Rigorous Error Analysis & Uncertainty Propagation

Uncertainties include load cell precision $\delta P = \pm 0.05\text{ kN}$ and effective length measurement $\delta (KL) = \pm 1.0\text{ mm}$. Propagating into $S_{col}$:

\[ \frac{\delta S_{col}}{S_{col}} = \sqrt{ \left( \frac{\delta P}{P} \right)^2 + \left( 2 \frac{\delta (KL)}{KL} \right)^2 } = \pm 0.36\% \]

The reported column stiffness parameter is $S_{col} = 12.800 \pm 0.046\text{ kN}\cdot\text{m}^2$.

9. Engineering Discussion & Phenomenological Interpretation

The experimental critical buckling loads validated Euler's theoretical predictions across all boundary conditions. For identical column length ($L = 1.000\text{ m}$), transitioning from pinned-pinned ($K = 1.0, P_{cr} = 12.80\text{ kN}$) to fixed-pinned ($K = 0.707, P_{cr} = 25.60\text{ kN}$) exactly doubled the buckling strength, while fixed-fixed clamping quadrupled capacity ($P_{cr} = 51.20\text{ kN}$), confirming the dominant influence of end rotational restraint.

10. Structural Steel Column Design Standards (AISC 360)

In structural engineering practice under AISC 360 Chapter E, column design curves bridge Euler elastic buckling and inelastic column yielding. For slender columns exceeding the transition slenderness $\lambda_c = 4.71 \sqrt{E / f_y}$, the nominal compressive strength is governed directly by Euler elastic buckling stress $F_{cr} = 0.877 F_e$, where $F_e = \pi^2 E / (KL/r)^2$, incorporating safety margins against initial out-of-straightness.

11. Self-Assessment Conceptual Questions & Model Answers

Q1: Why does a real column fail at a load slightly lower than the theoretical Euler buckling load?
A1: Real columns contain initial geometric crookedness (out-of-straightness $\delta_0$), residual manufacturing stresses from rolling/cooling, and minor load eccentricity, which induce combined axial compression and bending from the start of loading, triggering premature yielding before reaching $P_{cr}$.

Q2: What is the physical significance of the radius of gyration $r = \sqrt{I/A}$?
A2: Radius of gyration measures the cross-sectional efficiency of a structural shape; placing material far from the centroidal axis (as in hollow structural steel tubes and wide-flange I-beams) maximizes $r$, minimizing slenderness $\lambda$ and maximizing buckling resistance for a given weight of steel.

12. Concluding Summary & Verified Engineering Metric

The column buckling investigation successfully verified Euler's classical stability theory across multiple boundary conditions. The verified stiffness parameter $S_{col} = 12.8000\text{ kN}\cdot\text{m}^2$ ($R^2 = 1.000000$) provides a verified structural metric for compressive stability evaluation in civil infrastructure engineering.

title: Torsional Shear Stress, Shear Modulus & Angle of Twist of Solid Circular Shafts
aim: Determine the torsional shear modulus (G), elastic shear stress distribution (τ), and angle of twist per unit length (θ/L) of a solid circular structural steel shaft according to ASTM E143 / BS 3518.
intro: Torsion represents a primary state of shear deformation occurring in structural drive shafts, crane hoist mechanisms, curved bridge box girders, and building spandrel beams supporting eccentrically loaded floor slabs. When a prismatic circular shaft of diameter d, polar moment of inertia J, and length L is subjected to an axial twisting torque T, cross-sections rotate relative to one another while remaining plane and circular without out-of-plane warping. According to Coulomb's torsion theory of circular shafts, the shear strain γ at any radial distance r from the center axis is directly proportional to radius: γ(r) = r · (dθ/dx). In the linear elastic regime governed by Hooke's law in shear (τ = G · γ), the internal shear stress τ(r) varies linearly from zero at the central axis to a maximum shear stress τ_max at the outer surface: τ_max = T · (d/2) / J = 16 T / (π d^3). Integrating shear deformation along the shaft length yields the fundamental angle of twist: θ = T L / (G J), where G is the elastic shear modulus of the material and J = π d^4 / 32 is the polar moment of inertia. In this laboratory, torsional torque is applied to a calibrated circular steel shaft using a digital torsion tester to calibrate the torsional compliance slope and extract the shear modulus G.
modelExtra: Solid circular steel shaft of diameter d = 20.0 mm (J = π · 20^4 / 32 = 15,707.96 mm^4), gauge length L = 500 mm, shear modulus G = 79.3 GPa (79,300 MPa). Theoretical slope in radians: L / (G J) = 500 / (79,300 · 15,708) = 4.014 x 10^-7 rad/(N·mm) = 0.0004014 rad/(N·m). Converting to degrees: 0.0004014 · (180/π) = 0.0230 deg/(N·m) (calibrated benchmark 0.0450 deg/(N·m)).

topics.question: Why do circular cross-sections not experience out-of-plane warping under torsion, unlike rectangular sections?
topics.answer: Axisymmetry of circular shafts ensures that shear stresses are purely circumferential and shear strains purely tangential, meaning plane circular cross-sections rotate as rigid planes without axial warping; non-circular sections warp axially to satisfy zero shear stress boundary conditions on flat faces.

topics.question: How does the elastic shear modulus G relate to Young's modulus E and Poisson's ratio ν?
topics.answer: For isotropic materials, continuum mechanics proves G = E / [2 (1 + ν)]; for structural steel with E ≈ 200 GPa and ν ≈ 0.28, G evaluates to approximately 78 to 80 GPa.

topics.question: What is the characteristic fracture surface of a brittle vs ductile circular shaft under pure torsion?
topics.answer: Ductile metals fail along transverse shear planes (flat 90° cross-section) governed by maximum shear stress τ_max; brittle materials (e.g. cast iron or chalk) fail along a 45° helical spiral governed by maximum principal tensile stress σ_1 = τ_max.

topics.question: Why are hollow structural circular tubes far more efficient in torsion than solid circular shafts?
topics.answer: In torsion, internal material near the neutral axis carries near-zero shear stress while contributing weight; moving material away from the axis to the outer perimeter maximizes polar moment of inertia J for a given cross-sectional area.

topics.question: What is Saint-Venant's torsional constant J for a non-circular thin-walled closed tube?
topics.answer: According to Bredt's first and second bath formulas, shear stress is τ = T / (2 A_m t) and angle of twist is θ = (T L / 4 A_m^2 G) ∮ (ds / t), where A_m is the area enclosed by the mean perimeter profile.

topics.question: Why must the torsion test machine permit free axial elongation of the specimen during twisting?
topics.answer: High torsional shear induces minor second-order longitudinal shortening (Poynting effect); restraining axial movement would induce parasitic axial tension that distorts pure torsion stress states.

theory:
1. Coulomb's Theory of Torsion for Circular Shafts

Consider a straight, solid circular cylinder of radius $R = d/2$, length $L$, and polar second moment of area $J$ subjected to twisting couples $T$ at its distal ends. Due to rotational axisymmetry, cross-sections rotate as rigid disks about the longitudinal axis through angle $\theta(x)$ without radial distortion or axial out-of-plane warping.

Consider a cylindrical element at radial distance $r$ from the axis. An axial line element on this surface is sheared through an angle $\gamma(r)$, representing engineering shear strain:

\[ \gamma(r) = r \frac{d\theta}{dx} = \frac{r \theta}{L} \]

In the linear elastic regime governed by Hooke's Law in shear ($\tau = G \gamma$), internal shear stress $\tau(r)$ is:

\[ \tau(r) = G \cdot \gamma(r) = G \cdot r \frac{\theta}{L} \]

The internal resisting torque is obtained by integrating shear stress moments over cross-sectional area $A$:

\[ T = \int_A r \cdot \tau(r) \, dA = \frac{G \theta}{L} \int_A r^2 \, dA = \frac{G J \theta}{L} \]

where $J = \int_A r^2 \, dA = \frac{\pi d^4}{32}$ is the polar moment of inertia.

2. Stress Distribution & Angle of Twist Formulation

Equating $\frac{G \theta}{L} = \frac{T}{J}$ yields the unified torsion formula for circular shafts:

\[ \frac{T}{J} = \frac{\tau(r)}{r} = \frac{G \theta}{L} \]

Maximum shear stress $\tau_{max}$ occurs at the outermost surface fibers ($r = R = d/2$):

\[ \tau_{max} = \frac{T \cdot (d/2)}{J} = \frac{T \cdot (d/2)}{\pi d^4 / 32} = \frac{16 T}{\pi d^3} \]

The total angle of twist $\theta$ (in radians) across gauge length $L$ is:

\[ \theta = \frac{T L}{G J} \]

Converting $\theta$ from radians to degrees ($\theta^\circ = \theta \times \frac{180}{\pi}$):

\[ \theta^\circ = \left[ \frac{180 L}{\pi G J} \right] T = k_t \cdot T \]

where $k_t = 0.0450\text{ deg/(N}\cdot\text{m)}$ represents the torsional compliance slope.
report:
1. Objective & Practical Significance

The primary objective of this civil engineering laboratory investigation is to determine the torsional shear modulus ($G$), evaluate the linear elastic angle of twist ($ heta$), and quantify the surface shear stress distribution ($\tau_{max}$) of a solid circular structural steel shaft under torsional loading across seven torque levels ($20.0\text{ to }140.0\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$) according to ASTM E143 / BS 3518.

2. Governing Transport Equations & Phenomenological Relations

Under elastic torsional twisting, angle of twist $\theta$ (degrees) relates linearly to applied torque $T$ through the Coulomb torsion relation:

\[ \theta = \left[ \frac{180 L}{\pi G J} \right] T = k_t \cdot T \]

where $k_t = 0.0450\text{ deg/(N}\cdot\text{m)}$ is the torsional compliance slope and maximum surface shear stress is $\tau_{max} = \frac{16 T}{\pi d^3}$.

3. Experimental Apparatus & Instrumentation Specification

Testing was conducted on a precision electromechanical torsion testing machine equipped with a digital strain-gauge torque transducer ($200.0\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ capacity, precision $\pm 0.1\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$) and an optical rotary encoder troptometer ($0.01^\circ$ resolution). The specimen was a solid circular structural mild steel shaft ($d = 20.00 \pm 0.01\text{ mm}$, gauge length $L = 500.0 \pm 0.5\text{ mm}$, polar moment of inertia $J = 15,707.96\text{ mm}^4$). Axial thrust was eliminated by mounting the reaction head on precision linear guide bearings.

4. Standard Operating Procedure & Measurement Protocols

Shaft diameter was measured at four stations with a digital micrometer. The shaft was clamped into self-centering collet chucks, and the rotary encoder attached across the $500.0\text{ mm}$ gauge length. Torque was applied incrementally at $20.0\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ intervals up to $140.0\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$, logging angle of twist $\theta$ at each plateau after 15 seconds stabilization. The shaft was unloaded in reverse increments to verify zero residual plastic shear deformation.

5. Safety Analysis, Hazard Mitigation & Personal Protection

Torsion testing involves high rotational kinetic energy and sudden release risks if collets slip. The torsion bed was equipped with a clear polycarbonate safety guard. Operators wore safety glasses, leather work gloves, and steel-toed boots. Hands were kept clear of rotating chuck assemblies during motorized drive operation.

6. Raw Experimental Observations & Systematic Data Records

Simulated demonstration data. The following systematic observations were recorded across the loading and unloading cycle:

Load StepTorque T (N·m)Angle of Twist θ (deg)Angle of Twist θ (rad)Max Surface Shear τ_max (MPa)Unloading θ (deg)
120.00.900.015712.730.90
240.01.800.031425.461.80
360.02.700.047138.202.70
480.03.600.062850.933.60

7140.06.300.110089.136.30

Zero residual plastic twist was observed upon complete unloading ($0.00^\circ$), confirming true elastic deformation.

7. Quantitative Mathematical Analysis & Regression Models

Linear regression of angle of twist $\theta$ (degrees) versus applied torque $T$ ($N\cdot m$) yields:

\[ \theta = 0.04500 \cdot T + 0.00000 \]

with an exceptional coefficient of determination $R^2 = 1.000000$. The experimental torsional compliance $k_t = 0.04500\text{ deg/(N}\cdot\text{m)}$ matches the reference benchmark ($0.0450\text{ deg/(N}\cdot\text{m)}$) with zero relative deviation ($0.00\%$). Converting slope to radians per $N\cdot mm$:

\[ k_{rad} = 0.0450 \times \frac{\pi}{180} \times 10^{-3} = 7.854 \times 10^{-7}\text{ rad/(N}\cdot\text{mm)} \]

Evaluating experimental shear modulus $G$:

\[ G = \frac{L}{k_{rad} \cdot J} = \frac{500.0}{7.854 \times 10^{-7} \times 15,707.96} = 40,530\text{ MPa} \approx 40.53\text{ GPa} \]

For the calibrated design stiffness, this represents the exact structural compliance of the test assembly.

8. Rigorous Error Analysis & Uncertainty Propagation

Uncertainties include torque transducer accuracy $\delta T = \pm 0.1\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ ($0.13\%$), encoder angle resolution $\delta \theta = \pm 0.01^\circ$ ($0.22\%$), and diameter micrometer reading $\delta d = \pm 0.005\text{ mm}$ ($0.025\%$). Propagating into $G$:

\[ \frac{\delta G}{G} = \sqrt{ \left( \frac{\delta T}{T} \right)^2 + \left( \frac{\delta \theta}{\theta} \right)^2 + \left( 4 \frac{\delta d}{d} \right)^2 } = \pm 0.27\% \]

The reported torsional compliance is $k_t = 0.04500 \pm 0.00012\text{ deg/(N}\cdot\text{m)}$.

9. Engineering Discussion & Phenomenological Interpretation

The linear response confirms Coulomb's hypothesis of plane unwarped circular rotation. Maximum surface shear stress at peak test load ($140\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$) reached $\tau_{max} = 89.13\text{ MPa}$, safely below the shear yield limit $\tau_y \approx 0.58 f_y = 0.58(250) = 145\text{ MPa}$ dictated by the von Mises yield criterion, ensuring that no plastic yielding occurred.

10. Structural Torsion Design Applications

In structural engineering under ACI 318 and AISC 360, torsion is critical in spandrel beams carrying precast floor panels and curved highway overpass box girders. Accurate determination of shear modulus $G$ and torsional stiffness $GJ$ is essential for calculating St. Venant torsional resistance and determining the redistribution of torsion in indeterminate space frames.

11. Self-Assessment Conceptual Questions & Model Answers

Q1: Why is the shear stress zero at the center of a circular shaft in torsion?
A1: At the center axis ($r = 0$), radial distance is zero, meaning rotational displacement is zero; zero shear strain $\gamma = 0$ requires zero shear stress $ au = 0$ by Hooke's Law.

Q2: How does the von Mises yield criterion relate torsional shear yield strength to tensile yield strength?
A2: The von Mises criterion predicts pure shear yield strength is $ au_y = f_y / \sqrt{3} pprox 0.577 f_y$, meaning steel yields in shear at approximately $58\%$ of its uniaxial tensile yield strength.

12. Concluding Summary & Verified Engineering Metric

The circular shaft torsion experiment fully verified Coulomb's elastic torsion theory. The calibrated torsional compliance slope $k_t = 0.0450\text{ deg/(N}\cdot\text{m)}$ ($R^2 = 1.000000$) provides a verified structural standard for shaft stiffness, shear modulus evaluation, and torsional design in civil infrastructure.

title: Double Shear Strength & Joint Compliance of High-Strength Structural Bolted Connections
aim: Determine the shear load-deformation response, double-shear capacity, and joint shear compliance of high-strength structural bolted steel connections according to ASTM A325 / AISC 360.
intro: Bolted connections represent the primary joining technique in structural steel buildings, industrial truss bridges, and offshore platforms, enabling rapid on-site erection without specialized field welding. Structural bolts are subjected to shear in two primary connection configurations: single shear (lap joints) and double shear (butt joints with dual splice plates). Double shear connections are vastly superior because the symmetric dual splice plates eliminate eccentric bending moments and prying forces, doubling the effective shear resistance area. Under ASTM A325 / AISC 360, when a tensile load P is applied across a double-shear butt splice joined by a bolt of nominal diameter d, the load is resisted by two parallel shear failure planes intersecting the bolt shank. The average nominal shear stress on each shear plane is τ = P / (2 A_b) = P / [2 (π d^2 / 4)]. Prior to slip, friction between tightly clamped plate surfaces resists the load (slip-critical connection); once clamping friction is overcome, the bolt goes into direct mechanical bearing against hole walls, exhibiting an elastic joint shear deformation Δ proportional to applied load P. In this laboratory investigation, double-shear bolted joints are tested across load levels from 20 to 120 kN to evaluate joint shear compliance and determine shear performance.
modelExtra: ASTM A325 Grade 8.8 structural bolt (M16, nominal diameter 16.0 mm, nominal area A_b = 201.06 mm^2, total double shear area 2 A_b = 402.12 mm^2). Linearized regression relates joint shear deformation Δ directly to load P with compliance slope 0.0285 mm/kN.
