quiz.question: If a soil requires a penetration force of 3.34 kN at 2.54 mm, its California Bearing Ratio (CBR) is:

measureLabel: Record CBR piston penetration force P
theory:
1. Empirical Mechanics of the California Bearing Ratio

The CBR test is an empirical punching shear penetration test. When a flat-ended cylindrical steel piston of diameter $D_p = 49.63\text{ mm}$ (cross-sectional area $A_p = 1935.0\text{ mm}^2 = 3.0\text{ in}^2$) is forced into compacted soil at a constant displacement rate of $1.27\text{ mm/min}$, it generates a localized plastic bearing capacity failure zone directly beneath the circular punch.

According to Prandtl–Reissner plastic bearing capacity theory, the penetration resistance $P$ combines undrained shear cohesion $c_u$ and frictional resistance mobilized under surcharge confining pressure $q_{sur}$:

\[ q_p = \frac{P}{A_p} = c N_c + q_{sur} N_q + \frac{1}{2} \gamma D_p N_\gamma \]

Because soil exhibits strain-hardening and progressive shear mobilization, the resisting force $P$ increases monotonically with penetration depth $d$.

2. The CBR Formulation

The California Bearing Ratio ($CBR$) expresses measured resistance force $P$ as a percentage of the standard benchmark force $P_{std}$ established on crushed California limestone:

\[ CBR_{2.5} = \frac{P_{2.5}}{13.34\text{ kN}} \times 100\% \] \[ CBR_{5.0} = \frac{P_{5.0}}{20.00\text{ kN}} \times 100\% \]

Normally, $CBR_{2.5}$ governs. If $CBR_{5.0} > CBR_{2.5}$, the test is repeated; if confirmed, $CBR_{5.0}$ is adopted as the governing design metric.

3. Linear Penetration Stiffness Model

Across the linear penetration regime ($d = 1.5\text{ to }5.0\text{ mm}$), penetration resistance $P$ scales directly with displacement depth:

\[ P = k_{cbr} \cdot d \]

where $k_{cbr} = 2.4000\text{ kN/mm}$ represents the penetration stiffness slope. At standard depth $d = 2.50\text{ mm}$:

\[ P(2.5) = 2.4000 \times 2.50 = 6.000\text{ kN} \implies CBR_{2.5} = \frac{6.000}{13.34} \times 100\% = 44.98\% \approx 45.0\% \]

characteristic of high-strength crushed stone aggregate base course materials.
report:
1. Objective & Practical Significance

The primary objective of this geotechnical and highway engineering laboratory investigation is to evaluate the California Bearing Ratio ($CBR$), load-penetration stiffness, and 96-hour soaking swell of a compacted pavement base course material according to ASTM D1883 / AASHTO T193 across eight penetration depths ($d = 1.5\text{ to }5.0\text{ mm}$). By logging penetration resistance force $P$ and executing linear regression, we determine the penetration stiffness slope $k_{cbr}$ and calculate pavement structural thickness.

2. Governing Transport Equations & Phenomenological Relations

Piston penetration resistance force $P$ varies linearly with penetration depth $d$ according to:

\[ P = k_{cbr} \cdot d \]

where $k_{cbr} = 2.4000\text{ kN/mm}$. The California Bearing Ratio ($CBR$) at standard depths $2.5\text{ mm}$ and $5.0\text{ mm}$ is:

\[ CBR_{2.5} = \frac{P(2.5\text{ mm})}{13.34\text{ kN}} \times 100\%, \qquad CBR_{5.0} = \frac{P(5.0\text{ mm})}{20.00\text{ kN}} \times 100\% \]

3. Experimental Apparatus & Instrumentation Specification

Testing utilized a computerized electromechanical CBR testing machine equipped with a $50.0\text{ kN}$ load cell (precision $\pm 0.05\text{ kN}$) and a digital LVDT penetration transducer ($0.001\text{ mm}$ resolution). The hardened circular steel piston possessed diameter $D_p = 49.63 \pm 0.05\text{ mm}$ ($A_p = 1935.0\text{ mm}^2$). Specimen containment utilized a heavy steel CBR mold ($152.4\text{ mm}$ diameter, $177.8\text{ mm}$ height) with perforated baseplate and $4.54\text{ kg}$ slotted surcharge weights. Soaking swell was monitored with a mechanical dial gauge ($0.01\text{ mm}$ resolution).

4. Standard Operating Procedure & Measurement Protocols

Base course soil was blended at $OMC = 8.5\%$, compacted into the mold in five layers with 56 blows per layer of the $4.54\text{ kg}$ rammer, trimmed flush, and fitted with the $4.54\text{ kg}$ surcharge. The assembly was submerged in a water bath for 96 hours, recording $0.12\%$ volumetric swell. After 15 minutes gravity draining, the mold was mounted in the CBR machine with surcharge. The piston was seated at $45\text{ N}$, zeroed, and driven at $1.27\text{ mm/min}$, logging force $P$ at $0.5\text{ mm}$ increments up to $5.0\text{ mm}$.

5. Safety Analysis, Hazard Mitigation & Personal Protection

Heavy $4.54\text{ kg}$ surcharge weights and $12\text{ kg}$ steel compaction molds present pinch and lifting hazards. Operators wore steel-toed safety boots, leather gloves, and eye protection. Ergonomic two-handed lifting techniques were enforced.

6. Raw Experimental Observations & Systematic Data Records

Simulated demonstration data. The following systematic observations were recorded across the CBR penetration test (96-hr soaked condition):

7. Quantitative Mathematical Analysis & Regression Models

Linear regression of penetration resistance force $P$ versus penetration depth $d$ yields:

\[ P = 2.40000 \cdot d + 0.00000 \]

with an exceptional coefficient of determination $R^2 = 1.000000$. The experimental stiffness slope $k_{cbr} = 2.4000\text{ kN/mm}$ matches the design benchmark with zero relative deviation ($0.00\%$). Calculating California Bearing Ratio at standard depths:

\[ CBR_{2.5} = \frac{6.00\text{ kN}}{13.34\text{ kN}} \times 100\% = 44.98\% \] \[ CBR_{5.0} = \frac{12.00\text{ kN}}{20.00\text{ kN}} \times 100\% = 60.00\% \]

Because $CBR_{5.0} > CBR_{2.5}$, verification retesting confirmed the result; the governing design value is $CBR = 45.0\%$ (or $60.0\%$ under AASHTO 5.0 mm criteria), classifying the material as an exceptional crushed stone base course.

8. Rigorous Error Analysis & Uncertainty Propagation

Uncertainties include load cell reading $\delta P = \pm 0.05\text{ kN}$ ($0.83\%$) and LVDT penetration depth $\delta d = \pm 0.01\text{ mm}$ ($0.40\%$). Propagating into $CBR_{2.5}$:

\[ \frac{\delta CBR}{CBR} = \sqrt{ \left( \frac{\delta P}{P} \right)^2 + \left( \frac{\delta d}{d} \right)^2 } = \pm 0.92\% \]

The reported California Bearing Ratio is $CBR_{2.5} = 45.0 \pm 0.4\%$.

9. Engineering Discussion & Phenomenological Interpretation

The linear load-penetration response confirms immediate mechanical interlock without initial bedding concavity. High-density packing ($MDD = 2.15\text{ g/cm}^3$) of crushed limestone particles prevented punching shear collapse, mobilizing intense internal friction ($\phi > 42^\circ$). Minimal soaking swell ($0.12\% < 2.0\%$) ensures resistance to frost heave and moisture softening.

10. Flexible Pavement Structural Layer Sizing

Under the AASHTO flexible pavement design guide, resilient modulus is estimated as $M_r \approx 10.3 \times CBR = 10.3 \times 45.0 = 463.5\text{ MPa}$ ($67,200\text{ psi}$). This high modulus provides a layer structural coefficient $a_2 = 0.14$, permitting a significant reduction in required surface asphalt concrete thickness while maintaining design structural number ($SN$) over 20-year design traffic loads.

11. Self-Assessment Conceptual Questions & Model Answers

Q1: Why is an initial concave-upward load-penetration curve corrected by shifting the origin?
A1: Concave-upward curvature indicates surface roughness or a loose top layer before the piston engages true solid soil; drawing a tangent to the steepest linear portion and extending it to the zero-load axis resets the origin, ensuring penetration depths are measured from true solid contact.

Q2: What typical CBR values are observed for clay subgrades versus crushed rock base courses?
A2: Weak clay subgrades exhibit $CBR = 2\text{ to }5\%$; silty sands range from $10\text{ to }20\%$; well-graded crushed gravel subbases achieve $30\text{ to }50\%$; high-grade crushed limestone bases exceed $80\text{ to }100\%$.

12. Concluding Summary & Verified Engineering Metric

The California Bearing Ratio investigation verified the mechanical bearing resistance of the compacted pavement base material. The calibrated stiffness slope $k_{cbr} = 2.4000\text{ kN/mm}$ ($R^2 = 1.000000$), $CBR_{2.5} = 45.0\%$, and minimal swell of $0.12\%$ confirm full compliance with AASHTO specifications for heavy-duty highway pavement construction.

title: Flow Discharge Over Sharp-Crested Rectangular and 90° V-Notch Weirs (Discharge Coefficient C_d)
aim: Determine the discharge coefficient C_d and head-discharge relationships for sharp-crested rectangular and 90° triangular V-notch weirs in an open laboratory flume according to ISO 1438 / ASTM D5242.
intro: In open channel hydraulic engineering, sharp-crested weirs are fundamental obstruction structures utilized for precise discharge measurement, flood routing, irrigation water allotment, and storm runoff control. When water spills over an aerated sharp-crested plate, it detaches cleanly to form a free-falling jet known as a nappe. For a 90° triangular V-notch weir, the integration of elementary horizontal strips across the triangular geometry yields the theoretical discharge relation Q_th = (8/15) · tan(θ/2) · √(2g) · H^(5/2), where θ is the notch angle (90°), g is gravitational acceleration (9.81 m/s²), and H is upstream head above the vertex. Viscous boundary drag, surface tension, and contraction of streamlines reduce actual discharge relative to theoretical flow, necessitating a calibrated discharge coefficient C_d: Q = C_d · (8/15) · √(2g) · H^(5/2). For standard 90° brass notches, C_d typically ranges between 0.58 and 0.62, giving an empirical coefficient multiplier of approximately 1.38 m^(0.5)/s. Maintaining full aeration under the falling nappe is mandatory; insufficient venting creates an under-nappe partial vacuum that depresses pressure, sucks the jet downward, and induces catastrophic flow measurement errors up to 25%. In this laboratory flume experiment, water head H is accurately monitored with a vernier hook-and-point gauge at systematic discharge rates to establish the head-discharge rating curve and calibrate the weir discharge coefficient.
modelExtra: Calibrated on a precision brass 90° V-notch weir plate installed across an 8-meter tilting hydraulics flume. Linearized model relates discharge Q directly to head parameter H^(5/2) with slope 1.3800 m^(0.5)/s.

topics.question: Why is a triangular V-notch weir preferred over a rectangular weir for measuring low discharges?
topics.answer: At low flow rates, a rectangular weir produces an extremely shallow head H across a wide crest that is difficult to measure accurately; in contrast, a triangular notch concentrates flow toward its vertex, generating a substantial, easily measurable head even at minimal discharges.

topics.question: What physical phenomenon occurs if the under-nappe air cavity is not ventilated?
topics.answer: Air entrainment by falling water evacuates the pocket beneath the nappe, generating a sub-atmospheric partial vacuum that draws the jet downward (clinging nappe), increasing flow rate by up to 25% and invalidating standard rating equations.

topics.question: Why must head H be measured at least 4H upstream of the weir crest?
topics.answer: As water approaches the weir, streamlines accelerate and curvature depresses the free surface downward in a drawdown curve; measuring at least 4H upstream ensures head is recorded in the undisturbed hydrostatic flow zone.

topics.question: What is the theoretical head-discharge power exponent for a 90° V-notch weir versus a rectangular weir?
topics.answer: For a triangular V-notch weir, discharge scales with H^(5/2) (exponent 2.5); for a rectangular sharp-crested weir, discharge scales with H^(3/2) (exponent 1.5).

topics.question: How do surface tension and fluid viscosity affect the discharge coefficient C_d at very small heads (H < 20 mm)?
topics.answer: At very low heads, water clings to the crest face due to surface tension and viscous boundary layer drag, causing C_d to increase sharply and deviating from standard empirical calibration constants.

topics.question: What is the Cipolletti weir and what hydraulic design advantage does it offer?
topics.answer: A Cipolletti weir is a trapezoidal sharp-crested weir with side slopes of 1 horizontal to 4 vertical (14°); this specific slope exactly compensates for end contractions, making discharge directly proportional to crest length L.

precautions: Position the hook gauge point at least 4 times the maximum expected head upstream from the weir plate to avoid surface drawdown curvature.
Ensure side aeration vent pipes remain completely unobstructed to prevent under-nappe vacuum formation and clinging nappe behavior.
Wait until steady-state uniform conditions are established in the flume before logging head readings and volumetric tank collection intervals.
Keep the brass weir knife edge clean and free from oil films, algal accumulation, or mechanical nicks that distort jet contraction.

theory:
Hydraulic Formulation of Sharp-Crested Weirs

Sharp-crested weirs are open-channel control structures where flow separates from a sharp upstream edge. Consider an infinitesimal horizontal strip of height $dh$ at depth $h$ below the free surface over a triangular notch with included angle $\theta = 90^\circ$. The strip width is $b(h) = 2(H - h)\tan(\theta/2)$. Applying Torricelli's theorem for frictionless velocity $v(h) = \sqrt{2gh}$, theoretical elemental discharge is:

\[ dQ_{th} = b(h) \cdot dh \cdot \sqrt{2gh} = 2 (H - h) \tan\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right) \sqrt{2gh} \, dh \]

Integrating from $h = 0$ at the free surface to $h = H$ at the vertex:

\[ Q_{th} = 2 \tan\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right) \sqrt{2g} \int_0^H (H h^{1/2} - h^{3/2}) \, dh = \frac{8}{15} \tan\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right) \sqrt{2g} \, H^{5/2} \]

For a standard $90^\circ$ notch ($\theta = 90^\circ$, $\tan 45^\circ = 1$):

\[ Q_{th} = \frac{8}{15} \sqrt{2 \times 9.81} \, H^{5/2} = 2.361 \, H^{5/2} \]

Real fluids possess viscosity, surface tension, and streamline convergence, contracting the jet into a vena contracta. The actual volumetric discharge is modified by the discharge coefficient $C_d$:

\[ Q = C_d \frac{8}{15} \sqrt{2g} \, H^{5/2} = k_{weir} \cdot H^{5/2} \]

where $k_{weir} = C_d \times 2.361$. For a calibrated weir with $C_d = 0.5845$, $k_{weir} = 1.3800\text{ m}^{0.5}\text{/s}$.

Rectangular Weirs and End Contractions

For a rectangular weir of crest length $L$, the theoretical flow equation is $Q_{th} = \frac{2}{3} L \sqrt{2g} H^{3/2}$. When the weir crest is narrower than the flume width ($L < B$), side wall contractions pinch the stream inward. The Francis equation incorporates effective crest length: $L_{eff} = L - 0.1 n H$, where $n$ is the number of end contractions (usually $n = 2$).
report:
1. Objective & Practical Significance

This laboratory investigation evaluated the open-channel hydraulic characteristics of a sharp-crested $90^\circ$ triangular V-notch weir across six systematic head levels ($H^{5/2} = 0.05, 0.09, 0.13, 0.17, 0.21,$ and $0.25\text{ m}^{2.5}$). By measuring head upstream of the notch with a vernier hook gauge and measuring volumetric discharge in a calibrated sump tank, we calibrate the empirical discharge multiplier $k_{weir}$ and discharge coefficient $C_d$ according to ISO 1438 and ASTM D5242.

2. Governing Hydraulic & Transport Equations

Volumetric flow rate $Q$ through a sharp-crested triangular notch is governed by:

\[ Q = C_d \frac{8}{15} \tan\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right) \sqrt{2g} \, H^{5/2} = k_{weir} \cdot H^{5/2} \]

Linear regression of $Q$ against $H^{5/2}$ directly determines the weir rating slope $k_{weir} = 1.3800\text{ m}^{0.5}\text{/s}$, from which $C_d = k_{weir} / 2.361 = 0.5845$.

3. Experimental Apparatus & Instrumentation Specification

The experiment was conducted in an $8.0\text{ m}$ recirculating tilting glass flume ($0.30\text{ m}$ width, $0.45\text{ m}$ depth) equipped with an electromagnetic flow transmitter and sump. The weir plate was fabricated from mirror-polished $6.0\text{ mm}$ brass sheet with beveled $45^\circ$ downstream edges creating a $1.0\text{ mm}$ knife crest. Upstream water depth was monitored using a Mitutoyo digital point gauge (resolution $\pm 0.01\text{ mm}$) mounted $1.2\text{ m}$ upstream of the weir.

4. Standard Operating Procedure & Measurement Protocols

The flume was leveled horizontally. Water was impounded until the meniscus touched the apex of the notch, establishing datum $H_0$. Variable frequency pump drives established steady flows across target heads. Hook gauge coordinates were logged after flow stabilized. Discharge was confirmed via volumetric tank timing over 180-second collection intervals.

5. Safety Analysis, Hazard Mitigation & Personal Protection

High flume discharge presents water splash hazards and wet floor slip risks. Personnel wore slip-resistant footwear and safety glasses. Electrical pump motor housings were verified for GFCI grounding compliance.

6. Raw Experimental Observations & Systematic Data Records

Simulated demonstration data. The following systematic observations were recorded across six operational runs:

7. Quantitative Mathematical Analysis & Regression Models

Linear regression of volumetric discharge $Q$ against head parameter $H^{5/2}$ yields:

\[ Q = 1.38000 \cdot H^{5/2} + 0.00000 \]

with coefficient of determination $R^2 = 1.000000$. The experimental multiplier $k_{weir} = 1.3800\text{ m}^{0.5}\text{/s}$ precisely matches theoretical calibration ($0.00\%$ deviation). The resulting discharge coefficient is $C_d = 0.5845 \pm 0.0008$.

8. Rigorous Error Analysis & Uncertainty Propagation

Head measurement uncertainty is $\delta H = \pm 0.1\text{ mm}$, and volumetric tank time uncertainty is $\delta t = \pm 0.2\text{ s}$. Propagating into discharge $Q$:

\[ \frac{\delta Q}{Q} = \sqrt{ \left( \frac{5}{2} \frac{\delta H}{H} \right)^2 + \left( \frac{\delta V}{V} \right)^2 + \left( \frac{\delta t}{t} \right)^2 } = \pm 0.42\% \]

The calibrated discharge coefficient is $C_d = 0.5845 \pm 0.0025$.

9. Engineering Discussion & Phenomenological Interpretation

The experimental discharge exhibited strict power-law scaling with $H^{5/2}$, confirming classical potential flow theory. Boundary layer drag and 3D streamline contraction at the triangular vertex reduced flow to $58.45\%$ of ideal theoretical discharge. Constant aeration beneath the nappe maintained atmospheric pressure, preventing clinging nappe hysteresis.

10. Industrial Scale-Up & Field Hydrology Applications

In municipal stormwater catchments and wastewater treatment plants, $90^\circ$ V-notch weirs serve as standard compliance outfall flowmeters. Calibrating the discharge coefficient ensures regulatory reporting accuracy for effluent volumetric limits.

11. Self-Assessment Conceptual Questions & Model Answers

Q1: Why does a clinging nappe produce an overestimation of actual discharge?
A1: Without aeration, water draws out entrained air, creating a partial vacuum beneath the nappe that increases the effective pressure differential across the notch, pulling excess flow through the weir.

Q2: How does weir plate thickness affect measurement accuracy?
A2: A broad un-beveled crest causes the nappe to adhere to the flat top surface, acting as a broad-crested weir and dramatically changing the discharge coefficient.

12. Concluding Summary & Verified Engineering Metric

The 90° sharp-crested V-notch weir exhibited predictable hydraulic behavior. The verified discharge rating multiplier $k_{weir} = 1.3800\text{ m}^{0.5}\text{/s}$ ($R^2 = 1.000000$, $C_d = 0.5845$) validates ISO 1438 standards and provides an authoritative calibration reference for open-channel monitoring.

title: Hydraulic Jump Characteristics & Energy Dissipation in Open Channel Flow (Bélanger Equation)
aim: Investigate hydraulic jump formation, measure initial and sequent flow depths, compute head loss and energy dissipation efficiency, and verify the classical Bélanger momentum equation in a tilting flume.
targetName: Bélanger Sequent Depth Ratio Scaling Factor
intro: A hydraulic jump is a rapid, highly turbulent open-channel flow phenomenon occurring when supercritical flow (Froude number Fr > 1) abruptly transitions to subcritical flow (Fr < 1). In hydraulic infrastructure—including spillway stilling basins, sluice gate chutes, and canal drop structures—hydraulic jumps are intentionally generated as primary energy dissipators to convert catastrophic kinetic energy into internal thermal turbulence, preventing severe downstream bed scour and riverbank erosion. Applying the one-dimensional momentum conservation equation across the control volume while neglecting boundary friction yields the classical Bélanger equation (1828) relating initial supercritical depth y_1 to subcritical sequent (conjugate) depth y_2: y_2 / y_1 = 0.5 · [√(1 + 8·Fr_1²) - 1], where upstream Froude number Fr_1 = v_1 / √(g·y_1). Specific energy drops dramatically across the jump: head loss ΔE = E_1 - E_2 = (y_2 - y_1)³ / (4·y_1·y_2), representing macro-turbulent roller energy dissipation. Depending on initial Froude number Fr_1, jumps are categorized as undular (1.0 < Fr_1 < 1.7), weak (1.7 < Fr_1 < 2.5), oscillating (2.5 < Fr_1 < 4.5), steady (4.5 < Fr_1 < 9.0), or strong/choppy (Fr_1 > 9.0). In this laboratory flume experiment, supercritical flow is discharged beneath an adjustable sluice gate, and a downstream tailwater weir forces hydraulic jump stabilization to verify conjugate depths and energy dissipation efficiency.
modelExtra: Evaluated in an 8-meter tilting flume with adjustable sluice gate and tailwater weir. Linearized relationship correlates measured depth ratio directly to the Bélanger predictor with slope 1.0000.

topics.question: Why is the momentum equation used instead of the energy equation to derive the Bélanger relation?
topics.answer: Across a hydraulic jump, intense turbulent mixing, surface air entrainment, and macroscopic eddies dissipate a large unknown amount of internal energy as heat, making the energy equation indeterminate; however, external friction on the short flume boundary is negligible, allowing conservation of momentum to solve conjugate depths exactly.

topics.question: What is the physical meaning of the Froude number in open-channel hydraulics?
topics.answer: The Froude number Fr = v / √(gy) represents the ratio of inertial forces to gravitational forces, and equals the ratio of flow velocity v to the celerity c of elementary gravity surface waves.

topics.question: Why cannot an open-channel transition from subcritical to supercritical occur abruptly as a 'negative' hydraulic jump?
topics.answer: A negative jump would require specific energy to increase spontaneously without external energy input, violating the Second Law of Thermodynamics (ΔE would be negative).

topics.question: What happens to the location of the hydraulic jump if tailwater depth y_t is lower than theoretical sequent depth y_2?
topics.answer: The jump is swept downstream out of the stilling basin (repelled jump), causing high-velocity supercritical flow to attack the unprotected river bed.

topics.question: How do chute blocks, baffle piers, and end sills improve stilling basin performance?
topics.answer: They exert large drag forces on the incoming jet, stabilizing jump position, shortening required basin length by up to 50%, and accelerating turbulent dissipation.

topics.question: What is the primary operational hazard of an oscillating hydraulic jump (2.5 < Fr_1 < 4.5)?
topics.answer: Oscillating jumps generate severe surface wave surges that travel far downstream, overtopping canal banks and eroding riprap linings.

precautions: Position the upstream point gauge outside the curved drawdown surface immediately prior to the turbulent jump toe.
Wait for the downstream surface roller to fully settle before measuring sequent depth y_2 to prevent turbulent air froth bias.
Adjust tailwater weir gradually to prevent surging jump displacement that overtops flume glass sidewalls.
Ensure flume glass walls are clean to clearly observe the boundary separation line of the bottom turbulent roller.

quiz.question: A hydraulic jump occurs only when the upstream flow is:
quiz.explanation: A hydraulic jump is the abrupt transition from supercritical flow (Fr > 1) to subcritical flow (Fr < 1).

quiz.question: The classical Bélanger equation relates conjugate depths in a horizontal rectangular channel according to:
quiz.explanation: Applying momentum conservation in a rectangular channel yields y_2/y_1 = 0.5(√(1 + 8Fr_1²) - 1).

quiz.question: The energy dissipated as heat and turbulence across a rectangular hydraulic jump is given by:
quiz.explanation: Head loss across a rectangular hydraulic jump is exactly ΔE = (y_2 - y_1)³ / (4y_1y_2).

quiz.question: The optimal Froude number range for a well-behaved, highly efficient steady hydraulic jump is:
quiz.explanation: For 4.5 < Fr_1 < 9.0, a steady jump forms with stable roller action and 45%–70% energy dissipation.

theory:
Governing Momentum Principle in Rapid Open Channel Transitions

In a horizontal rectangular flume of width $B$, neglecting boundary shear stress over the short jump length $L_j \approx 6 y_2$, hydrostatic pressure forces and momentum flux balance:

\[ P_1 - P_2 = M_2 - M_1 \] \[ \frac{1}{2} \rho g B y_1^2 - \frac{1}{2} \rho g B y_2^2 = \rho Q (v_2 - v_1) \]

Substituting continuity $Q = B y_1 v_1 = B y_2 v_2$ and dividing by $\frac{1}{2} \rho g B$:

\[ y_1^2 - y_2^2 = \frac{2 q^2}{g} \left( \frac{1}{y_2} - \frac{1}{y_1} \right) = \frac{2 q^2 (y_1 - y_2)}{g y_1 y_2} \]

where $q = Q/B$ is discharge per unit width. Factoring $(y_1 - y_2)(y_1 + y_2)$ and dividing by $(y_1 - y_2)$ (since $y_1 \neq y_2$):

\[ y_1 + y_2 = \frac{2 q^2}{g y_1 y_2} = \frac{2 v_1^2 y_1}{g y_2} \]

Multiplying through by $y_2/y_1^2$ and defining upstream Froude number $Fr_1^2 = v_1^2 / (g y_1)$:

\[ \left( \frac{y_2}{y_1} \right)^2 + \left( \frac{y_2}{y_1} \right) - 2 Fr_1^2 = 0 \]

Solving the quadratic equation for positive depth ratio yields the historic Bélanger equation:

\[ \frac{y_2}{y_1} = \frac{1}{2} \left( \sqrt{1 + 8 Fr_1^2} - 1 \right) \]

Energy Loss and Dissipation Efficiency

Specific energy at sections 1 and 2 is $E_1 = y_1 + \frac{v_1^2}{2g}$ and $E_2 = y_2 + \frac{v_2^2}{2g}$. The head loss across the jump is:

\[ \Delta E = E_1 - E_2 = \frac{(y_2 - y_1)^3}{4 y_1 y_2} \]

The relative energy dissipation efficiency is $\eta = \Delta E / E_1$.
report:
1. Objective & Practical Significance

This laboratory investigation evaluated hydraulic jump formation, conjugate depth ratios, and turbulent energy dissipation in a glass-walled open tilting flume across six systematically varied Froude numbers ($Fr_1 = 1.83$ to $5.45$, corresponding to Bélanger predictors $1.5$ to $4.5$). Experimental findings verify the classical Bélanger momentum equation and provide design parameters for spillway stilling basins.

2. Governing Momentum & Energy Equations

The conjugate depth ratio in a horizontal rectangular channel is predicted by:

\[ \frac{y_2}{y_1} = \frac{1}{2} \left( \sqrt{1 + 8 Fr_1^2} - 1 \right) \]

Specific energy head loss dissipated into turbulent heat is:

\[ \Delta E = E_1 - E_2 = \frac{(y_2 - y_1)^3}{4 y_1 y_2} \]

3. Experimental Apparatus & Instrumentation Specification

Testing utilized an $8.0\text{ m}$ recirculating flume ($0.30\text{ m}$ width, $0.45\text{ m}$ depth) with stainless steel bed and tempered glass walls. Flow was throttled through a precision vertical sluice gate and stabilized downstream by an adjustable hinged tailwater weir. Depths $y_1$ and $y_2$ were measured with Mitutoyo digital point gauges ($\pm 0.05\text{ mm}$). Velocity profiles were captured with a United Sensor Pitot-static tube.

4. Standard Operating Procedure & Measurement Protocols

Flume bed was leveled horizontally. Supercritical flow was established beneath the sluice gate. Tailwater was raised until the jump stabilized $2.5\text{ m}$ downstream of the gate. Supercritical depth $y_1$ was measured upstream of the jump toe, and subcritical depth $y_2$ downstream of the surface roller. Discharge $Q$ was recorded from an electromagnetic flowmeter.

5. Safety Analysis, Hazard Mitigation & Personal Protection

Violent surface roller splashing can wet flume walkways. Operators wore non-slip boots and safety goggles. Clear acrylic flume spray hoods were placed over the hydraulic jump section.

6. Raw Experimental Observations & Systematic Data Records

Simulated demonstration data. The following systematic observations were recorded for channel width $B = 0.300\text{ m}$:

7. Quantitative Mathematical Analysis & Regression Models

Linear regression of measured sequent depth ratio $y_2/y_1$ versus the Bélanger predictor yields:

\[ \frac{y_2}{y_1} = 1.00000 \cdot F(Fr_1) + 0.00000 \]

with an ideal coefficient of determination $R^2 = 1.000000$. The experimental scaling factor $k_{jump} = 1.0000$ exhibits zero deviation ($0.00\%$) from theoretical momentum conservation.

8. Rigorous Error Analysis & Uncertainty Propagation

Measurement uncertainty in flow depths is $\delta y = \pm 0.2\text{ mm}$, and discharge uncertainty is $\delta Q = \pm 0.5\%$. Propagating into $Fr_1$ and depth ratio:

\[ \frac{\delta (y_2/y_1)}{y_2/y_1} = \sqrt{ \left( \frac{\delta y_2}{y_2} \right)^2 + \left( \frac{\delta y_1}{y_1} \right)^2 } = \pm 0.85\% \]

The empirical depth ratio confirms the Bélanger relationship within experimental tolerance.

9. Engineering Discussion & Phenomenological Interpretation

For low Froude numbers ($Fr_1 = 1.83$), the jump exhibited a gentle undulating wave surface with low energy loss ($\Delta E / E_1 = 9.2\%$). As Froude number reached $4.90$, intense turbulent rollers formed with violent air entrainment, dissipating up to $52.4\%$ of initial specific energy. The bottom roller maintained stable attachment to the flume floor.

10. Hydraulic Infrastructure Design & Stilling Basins

In dam spillway design (USBR Type II and III basins), stilling basin floor elevation must be set below downstream riverbed level so that tailwater depth $y_t$ matches or slightly exceeds sequent depth $y_2$, locking the jump securely inside the concrete apron under design flood discharge.

11. Self-Assessment Conceptual Questions & Model Answers

Q1: Why is boundary friction negligible in the Bélanger momentum balance?
A1: The hydraulic jump occurs over an extremely short distance ($L_j \approx 6 y_2$), making the boundary shear force tiny compared to the enormous hydrostatic pressure difference and momentum flux change.

Q2: What is the consequence if downstream tailwater depth exceeds sequent depth y_2?
A2: The jump is drowned or submerged; the high-velocity supercritical jet plunges beneath the deep water surface as a submerged drowned jet, reducing bottom turbulence dissipation.

12. Concluding Summary & Verified Engineering Metric

The hydraulic jump investigation verified momentum conservation in open-channel flow. The measured conjugate depth ratio matched the Bélanger equation with scaling slope $k_{jump} = 1.0000$ ($R^2 = 1.000000$), confirming that stilling basin design equations accurately predict conjugate depths and turbulent dissipation.

title: Manning Roughness Coefficient Determination in an Open Tilting Flume (Uniform Flow)
aim: Determine Manning's roughness coefficient (n) and Chezy's coefficient (C) for smooth and artificially roughened open channels under steady uniform flow conditions across variable bed slopes.
intro: In open channel hydraulic design—governing storm drainage canals, aqueducts, river floodways, and natural waterways—the resistance to gravity-driven steady uniform flow is parameterized by empirical friction coefficients. Formulated by Irish engineer Robert Manning in 1889, the Manning equation expresses mean flow velocity as v = (1/n) · R^(2/3) · S^(1/2), where v is mean cross-sectional velocity (m/s), n is Manning's roughness coefficient (s/m^(1/3)), R = A / P is hydraulic radius (wetted flow area A divided by wetted perimeter P), and S is channel bed slope (equal to energy slope S_f in steady uniform flow). Manning's n embodies surface roughness of channel boundaries, form resistance from sand ripples or dunes, vegetation drag, and channel planform sinuosity. Smooth painted steel or planed timber exhibits n ≈ 0.010 to 0.012 s/m^(1/3); smooth troweled concrete has n ≈ 0.013 to 0.015 s/m^(1/3); gravel-bed mountain streams range from n = 0.030 to 0.050 s/m^(1/3); and heavily vegetated floodplains exceed n = 0.080 s/m^(1/3). In this laboratory flume experiment, uniform flow depth y_0 is maintained across varying bed slopes S and discharges Q. Plotting mean velocity v against the compound hydraulic geometric parameter R^(2/3) · S^(1/2) directly yields the reciprocal of Manning's roughness coefficient (1/n), enabling precise verification of concrete flume boundary resistance.
modelExtra: Evaluated on smooth finished concrete flume bed (n = 0.0150 s/m^(1/3)). Linear regression correlates mean velocity v directly to hydraulic parameter R^(2/3)·S^(1/2) with slope 66.6667 m^(1/3)/s.

topics.question: What is steady uniform flow in an open channel?
topics.answer: Steady uniform flow occurs when flow depth, velocity, and discharge remain strictly constant with respect to both time (steady) and longitudinal distance along the channel (uniform), meaning bed slope S_0, water surface slope S_w, and energy grade line slope S_f are identical and parallel.

topics.question: How is the hydraulic radius R defined and why is it hydraulically significant?
topics.answer: Hydraulic radius is defined as wetted cross-sectional area A divided by wetted perimeter P (R = A/P); it represents the effective depth of flow that resists friction, with larger R values producing less frictional resistance per unit volume.

topics.question: What is the relationship between Manning's n, Chezy's C, and the Darcy-Weisbach friction factor f?
topics.answer: Under steady uniform flow, the three resistance coefficients are related by C = R^(1/6) / n = √(8g / f), demonstrating that all three represent boundary shear resistance.

topics.question: Why is Manning's equation dimensionally non-homogeneous?
topics.answer: In SI units, velocity is in m/s while R^(2/3)S^(1/2) is in m^(2/3), meaning Manning's n must carry implicit dimensions of s/m^(1/3) (or s·m^(-1/3)), requiring a conversion factor k = 1.486 when using US customary units (ft/s and ft).

topics.question: What cross-sectional shape is the most hydraulically efficient for a rectangular channel?
topics.answer: A rectangular channel achieves maximum hydraulic efficiency (maximum discharge for a given area) when flow depth equals half the channel bottom width (y = B/2), resulting in hydraulic radius R = y/2.

topics.question: How does sediment transport or bedform formation alter Manning's n in alluvial rivers?
topics.answer: As velocity increases, sand beds transition from flat beds (low n) to ripples and large dunes (high form drag, n increases up to 0.045), then plane beds (lower n), and finally anti-dunes with breaking surface waves (high resistance).

precautions: Verify that water surface slope exactly matches channel bed slope (uniform flow condition) by checking depth gauges at three flume stations.
Ensure tailwater control gate is trimmed carefully to eliminate backwater (M1 curve) or drawdown (M2 curve) surface distortions.

Allow minimum 5 minutes after slope adjustment for flume hydrodynamic equilibrium before logging depth and discharge.

quiz.explanation: To make the Manning equation dimensionally consistent with v in m/s, n has dimensions of seconds per meter to the one-third power (s/m^(1/3)).

quiz.explanation: Hydraulic radius R = Area / Wetted Perimeter = (B · y) / (B + 2y).

measureLabel: Record open channel uniform flow velocity
theory:
The Manning Uniform Flow Formulation

Uniform flow represents the fundamental equilibrium state where gravitational driving force along channel slope equals resisting boundary shear drag. For a channel slice of length $L$, cross-sectional area $A$, and bed slope $S = \sin\theta \approx \tan\theta$:

\[ F_{gravity} = \rho g A L S \]

The resisting shear force along the wetted perimeter $P$ is:

\[ F_{friction} = \tau_0 P L \]

Equating driving and resisting forces gives boundary shear stress $\tau_0$:

\[ \tau_0 = \rho g \frac{A}{P} S = \rho g R S \]

In 1769, Antoine Chézy related boundary shear to velocity squared $\tau_0 = \frac{1}{2} C_f \rho v^2$, yielding $v = C \sqrt{R S}$, where $C$ is Chézy's coefficient. In 1889, Robert Manning synthesized empirical datasets, demonstrating that $C$ varies with hydraulic radius to the one-sixth power: $C = \frac{1}{n} R^{1/6}$. Substituting into Chézy's equation yields the Manning equation:

\[ v = \frac{1}{n} R^{2/3} S^{1/2} \]

Volumetric discharge is $Q = A v = \frac{1}{n} A R^{2/3} S^{1/2}$.

Hydraulic Best Section Geometry

For a rectangular channel of fixed area $A = B y$, wetted perimeter is $P = B + 2y = \frac{A}{y} + 2y$. Minimizing perimeter with respect to depth $\frac{dP}{dy} = -\frac{A}{y^2} + 2 = 0$ yields $A = 2y^2$, or $B = 2y$. The most hydraulically efficient rectangular channel has a width twice its depth, with hydraulic radius $R = \frac{y}{2}$.
report:
1. Objective & Practical Significance

This laboratory investigation determined the Manning roughness coefficient $n$ and verified uniform flow mechanics in an open tilting flume across six systematic hydraulic geometry conditions ($R^{2/3} S^{1/2} = 0.010$ to $0.035\text{ m}^{2/3}$). The empirical roughness coefficient was evaluated against international design benchmarks for smooth concrete channel linings.

2. Governing Transport Equations & Phenomenological Relations

Steady uniform open channel flow is governed by the Manning equation:

\[ v = \frac{1}{n} R^{2/3} S^{1/2} \]

Linear regression of mean velocity $v$ against the composite parameter $X = R^{2/3} S^{1/2}$ yields slope $m = 1/n$, from which Manning's roughness coefficient is computed as $n = 1/m$.

3. Experimental Apparatus & Instrumentation Specification

Testing utilized an $8.0\text{ m}$ recirculating tilting glass flume ($0.30\text{ m}$ width) with a smooth finished concrete bed. Slope $S$ was monitored with a Mitutoyo digital inclinometer ($\pm 0.0001\text{ rad}$). Water depth $y_0$ was logged using vernier depth gauges ($\pm 0.05\text{ mm}$) mounted on a longitudinal carriage. Volumetric discharge $Q$ was recorded from an electromagnetic flowmeter.

4. Standard Operating Procedure & Measurement Protocols

The flume was adjusted to target slope $S$. Discharge $Q$ was set, and the tailwater gate trimmed until depth was uniform along the flume length ($dy/dx = 0$). Normal depth $y_0$ was recorded. Cross-sectional area $A = B y_0$, wetted perimeter $P = B + 2y_0$, and hydraulic radius $R = A/P$ were calculated. Mean velocity $v = Q/A$ was computed for each trial.

5. Safety Analysis, Hazard Mitigation & Personal Protection

Motorized flume jacking presents pinch hazards. Operators verified that travel limits were clear. Flume walkways were maintained dry to prevent slipping.

6. Raw Experimental Observations & Systematic Data Records

Simulated demonstration data. The following systematic observations were recorded for flume width $B = 0.300\text{ m}$:

7. Quantitative Mathematical Analysis & Regression Models

Linear regression of mean flow velocity $v$ against $R^{2/3} S^{1/2}$ yields:

\[ v = 66.66670 \cdot [R^{2/3} S^{1/2}] + 0.00000 \]

with coefficient of determination $R^2 = 1.000000$. The empirical slope $1/n = 66.6667\text{ m}^{1/3}\text{/s}$ yields a verified Manning roughness coefficient of $n = 0.01500\text{ s/m}^{1/3}$, exactly matching the design benchmark for smooth finished concrete.

8. Rigorous Error Analysis & Uncertainty Propagation

Depth uncertainty is $\delta y = \pm 0.1\text{ mm}$, slope uncertainty is $\delta S = \pm 0.00005$, and discharge uncertainty is $\delta Q = \pm 0.5\%$. Propagating into $n$:

\[ \frac{\delta n}{n} = \sqrt{ \left( \frac{\delta Q}{Q} \right)^2 + \left( \frac{5}{3} \frac{\delta y}{y} \right)^2 + \left( \frac{1}{2} \frac{\delta S}{S} \right)^2 } = \pm 1.15\% \]

The reported Manning roughness is $n = 0.0150 \pm 0.0002\text{ s/m}^{1/3}$.

9. Engineering Discussion & Phenomenological Interpretation

The linear velocity response confirms that gravitational driving head is balanced by turbulent boundary shear across the Reynolds number range ($Re = 45,000$ to $160,000$). Equivalent Chézy coefficient evaluated at median hydraulic radius $R = 0.056\text{ m}$ is $C = R^{1/6}/n = 41.2\text{ m}^{1/2}\text{/s}$, and Darcy-Weisbach friction factor is $f = 8g/C^2 = 0.046$.

10. Storm Drainage & Canal Design Applications

Engineers sizing drainage canals and highway culverts apply $n = 0.015$ for precast concrete pipes. An accurate roughness coefficient prevents undersizing that triggers urban surface flooding, or oversizing that causes excessive excavation costs.

11. Self-Assessment Conceptual Questions & Model Answers

Q1: Why does Manning's n decrease slightly as flow depth increases in concrete channels?
A1: At greater depths, boundary shear along the perimeter represents a smaller proportion of total cross-sectional flow volume, meaning relative surface roughness $k_s/R$ decreases.

Q2: How does vegetative growth in unlined earth channels affect the stage-discharge rating curve?
A2: Flexible grasses bend and flatten at high velocities, reducing $n$ from $0.050$ at low flow to $0.030$ during flood peaks, introducing non-linear rating curve behavior.

12. Concluding Summary & Verified Engineering Metric

The Manning open-channel flume investigation verified uniform flow resistance mechanics. The calibrated reciprocal roughness slope $1/n = 66.6667\text{ m}^{1/3}\text{/s}$ ($R^2 = 1.000000$) establishes a verified Manning's roughness coefficient $n = 0.0150\text{ s/m}^{1/3}$ for concrete open channel conveyance.

title: Frictional Head Loss in Pressurized Circular Conduits (Darcy-Weisbach Friction Factor)
aim: Measure frictional head losses (h_f) in smooth and rough pipes over a wide range of flow velocities, compute the Darcy-Weisbach friction factor f, and validate the Moody diagram and Colebrook-White equation.
intro: In civil municipal water distribution networks, cross-country transmission mains, wastewater force mains, and industrial cooling loops, pressurized fluid flow experiences continuous energy dissipation due to viscous boundary layer shear and turbulent momentum exchange. Formulated by Henry Darcy and Julius Weisbach in the mid-19th century, the Darcy-Weisbach equation provides the fundamental theoretical basis for pipe friction head loss: h_f = f · (L / D) · (v² / 2g), where h_f is head loss (m of fluid), f is the dimensionless Darcy friction factor, L is pipe length (m), D is internal pipe diameter (m), v is mean flow velocity (m/s), and g is gravitational acceleration (9.81 m/s²). Unlike empirical formulas such as Hazen-Williams, the Darcy-Weisbach equation is dimensionally rigorous and universally applicable to any Newtonian fluid. In laminar flow (Reynolds number Re = ρvD/μ < 2000), friction factor depends strictly on viscous dissipation: f = 64 / Re (Hagen-Poiseuille law). In turbulent flow (Re > 4000), f depends on both Reynolds number and relative wall roughness (ε/D), as characterized by the Colebrook-White implicit equation and Moody diagram. In this laboratory pipe apparatus, differential pressure piezometers record frictional head loss h_f across a 5.0 m test length of smooth copper tubing (D = 24.0 mm) across velocities from 0.5 to 3.0 m/s to calibrate the quadratic resistance coefficient fL/(2gD) = 0.4200 s²/m.
modelExtra: Tested on 5.0 m test length of smooth copper pipe (internal diameter D = 24.0 mm). Quadratic model relates head loss h_f directly to velocity squared v² with resistance slope 0.4200 s²/m (yielding f = 0.0197).

topics.question: How does the Darcy-Weisbach equation differ from the empirical Hazen-Williams formula?
topics.answer: The Darcy-Weisbach equation is dimensionally rigorous, derived from fluid mechanics principles, and applies to any fluid at any temperature, whereas Hazen-Williams is an empirical formula valid only for water at ordinary room temperatures and fails for high-viscosity fluids or non-turbulent flow.

topics.question: What is the physical significance of the laminar sublayer in turbulent pipe flow?
topics.answer: In turbulent flow, a thin laminar sublayer clings to the pipe wall; if surface roughness asperities ε are smaller than this sublayer (hydraulically smooth), friction factor f depends solely on Re; if asperities pierce through the sublayer (hydraulically rough), f depends solely on relative roughness ε/D.

topics.question: Why is head loss directly proportional to velocity v in laminar flow, but proportional to v² in fully turbulent flow?
topics.answer: In laminar flow, energy is dissipated by linear viscous shear stresses between fluid laminas (Poiseuille flow, h_f ∝ v); in turbulent flow, energy is dissipated by inertial momentum transfer of macroscopic eddies, scaling with kinetic energy (v²/2g).

topics.question: What is the Moody diagram and what are its four flow regimes?
topics.answer: The Moody diagram plots friction factor f against Reynolds number Re across relative roughness curves: (1) Laminar regime (Re < 2000, f = 64/Re); (2) Critical transition zone (2000 < Re < 4000); (3) Transition turbulent regime (f depends on both Re and ε/D); and (4) Fully rough turbulent regime (f is horizontal and constant with respect to Re).

topics.question: How does water temperature influence frictional head loss in water supply pipelines?
topics.answer: Warmer water has lower dynamic viscosity μ, increasing Reynolds number Re, which slightly decreases the friction factor f in smooth pipes and reduces head loss.

topics.question: What is the Colebrook-White equation and why is it implicit in friction factor f?
topics.answer: The Colebrook-White equation (1939) is 1/√f = -2 log₁₀ [ (ε/3.7D) + (2.51 / Re√f) ]; it is implicit because f appears on both sides of the equation, requiring iterative numerical solution (or approximation via the Swamee-Jain formula).

precautions: Thoroughly bleed all air bubbles from manometer impulse lines prior to recording pressure differentials.
Ensure pressure taps are located at least 50 pipe diameters downstream of elbows and valves to allow fully developed flow profiles.
Verify water temperature remains stable during testing to avoid viscosity shifts that alter Reynolds number.
Inspect pressure tap piezometer holes to ensure no burrs or internal drill shavings protrude into the pipe flow stream.

quiz.question: In the Darcy-Weisbach equation h_f = f · (L/D) · (v² / 2g), the friction factor f in laminar flow is:
quiz.explanation: For laminar pipe flow (Re < 2000), Poiseuille's law yields exact friction factor f = 64 / Re.

quiz.question: In the fully rough turbulent regime of the Moody chart, the friction factor f depends on:
options: Both Reynolds number and pipe length
quiz.explanation: In fully rough turbulent flow, roughness asperities completely break up the laminar sublayer, making f independent of Re and solely a function of relative roughness ε/D.

quiz.question: If flow velocity through a pressurized pipeline is doubled in turbulent flow, the frictional head loss increases by a factor of:
quiz.explanation: Since head loss scales quadratically with velocity (h_f ∝ v²), doubling velocity quadruples head loss (2² = 4).

quiz.question: Pressure tap orifices drilled into the pipe wall must be:
options: Drilled flush and smooth with the inner wall

theory:
Darcy-Weisbach Momentum Balance & Friction Factor

For fully developed steady flow of an incompressible fluid in a horizontal circular pipe of diameter $D$ and length $L$, the force balance between net pressure driving force and wall shear resistance $\tau_w$ is:

\[ (P_1 - P_2) \frac{\pi D^2}{4} = \tau_w (\pi D L) \] \[ \Delta P = \frac{4 L}{D} \tau_w \]

Expressing pressure drop as head loss $h_f = \frac{\Delta P}{\rho g}$ and introducing the Darcy friction factor definition $\tau_w = \frac{1}{8} f \rho v^2$:

\[ h_f = f \frac{L}{D} \frac{v^2}{2g} \]

In laminar flow ($Re < 2000$), Poiseuille flow velocity profile $u(r) = 2v(1 - 4r^2/D^2)$ gives wall shear $\tau_w = \mu |du/dr|_{r=D/2} = 8\mu v / D$. Substituting into the Darcy equation yields:

\[ f = \frac{64}{Re} \quad \text{where} \quad Re = \frac{\rho v D}{\mu} \]

Turbulent Flow and the Colebrook-White Equation

For turbulent flow ($Re > 4000$), friction factor is governed by the implicit Colebrook-White equation:

\[ \frac{1}{\sqrt{f}} = -2 \log_{10} \left( \frac{\epsilon / D}{3.7} + \frac{2.51}{Re \sqrt{f}} \right) \]

For smooth pipes ($\epsilon/D \to 0$), the formula simplifies to the Prandtl-von Kármán smooth pipe law. The composite resistance parameter $k = fL / (2gD)$ allows direct linear estimation of $h_f$ versus $v^2$.
report:
1. Objective & Practical Significance

This laboratory investigation evaluated frictional head loss in a smooth circular copper pipe ($D = 24.0\text{ mm}$, $L = 5.0\text{ m}$) across six systematic flow velocities ($v = 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5,$ and $3.0\text{ m/s}$). Testing verifies the quadratic velocity dependence of the Darcy-Weisbach equation, determines the experimental friction factor $f$, and validates hydraulic pipe design standards.

2. Governing Mechanical & Energy Equations

Frictional head loss in circular conduits is governed by:

\[ h_f = f \frac{L}{D} \frac{v^2}{2g} = k_{pipe} \cdot v^2 \]

where $k_{pipe} = \frac{f L}{2g D}$. Plotting $h_f$ against $v^2$ yields the linear slope $k_{pipe} = 0.4200\text{ s}^2\text{/m}$, from which the Darcy friction factor is computed as $f = k_{pipe} \cdot \frac{2g D}{L}$.

3. Experimental Apparatus & Instrumentation Specification

Testing utilized a closed-loop hydraulics test rig equipped with a $5.0\text{ m}$ straight length of drawn copper tube ($D = 24.00 \pm 0.05\text{ mm}$). Differential pressure was measured across piezometer taps using an inverted pressurized air-water manometer ($\pm 1.0\text{ mm}$) and a Rosemount digital differential pressure transmitter. Volumetric flow rate was monitored with an Endress+Hauser electromagnetic flowmeter.

4. Standard Operating Procedure & Measurement Protocols

Piezometer impulse lines were purged of trapped air. Flow velocity was adjusted from $0.5$ to $3.0\text{ m/s}$ using an inverter pump control. At each step, steady differential head loss $h_f$, water temperature ($T = 20.0^\circ\text{C}$, $\nu = 1.004 \times 10^{-6}\text{ m}^2\text{/s}$), and volumetric discharge $Q$ were recorded.

5. Safety Analysis, Hazard Mitigation & Personal Protection

High-pressure piping systems present leak and pressurized spray risks. Piping joints were pressure-rated to $10\text{ bar}$. Operators wore safety glasses and non-slip footwear.

6. Raw Experimental Observations & Systematic Data Records

Simulated demonstration data. The following systematic observations were recorded for pipe diameter $D = 0.024\text{ m}$ and length $L = 5.0\text{ m}$:

7. Quantitative Mathematical Analysis & Regression Models

Linear regression of head loss $h_f$ versus velocity squared $v^2$ yields:

\[ h_f = 0.42000 \cdot v^2 + 0.00000 \]

with an exceptional coefficient of determination $R^2 = 1.000000$. The experimental resistance slope $k_{pipe} = 0.4200\text{ s}^2\text{/m}$ yields Darcy friction factor:

\[ f = 0.4200 \times \frac{2 \times 9.81 \times 0.024}{5.0} = 0.01978 \]

which matches the Blasius smooth pipe prediction $f = 0.3164 / Re^{0.25} = 0.0198$ at median $Re = 35,850$ within $0.1\%$.

8. Rigorous Error Analysis & Uncertainty Propagation

Manometer deflection uncertainty is $\delta h = \pm 0.002\text{ m}$, diameter uncertainty is $\delta D = \pm 0.05\text{ mm}$, and velocity uncertainty is $\delta v = \pm 0.01\text{ m/s}$. Propagating into $f$:

\[ \frac{\delta f}{f} = \sqrt{ \left( \frac{\delta h}{h} \right)^2 + \left( \frac{\delta D}{D} \right)^2 + \left( 2 \frac{\delta v}{v} \right)^2 + \left( \frac{\delta L}{L} \right)^2 } = \pm 1.25\% \]

The reported Darcy friction factor is $f = 0.0198 \pm 0.0002$.

9. Engineering Discussion & Phenomenological Interpretation

The quadratic relationship between $h_f$ and $v$ confirmed fully turbulent pipe flow across all tested velocities ($Re = 11,950$ to $71,700$). Because drawn copper is hydraulically smooth, the laminar sublayer thickness ($\delta_v \approx 50\mu / \sqrt{\rho \tau_w} \approx 40\text{ }\mu\text{m}$) completely submerged copper wall micro-asperities ($\epsilon \approx 1.5\text{ }\mu\text{m}$), confirming smooth pipe behavior.

10. Pipeline Infrastructure & Municipal Network Applications

Water transmission engineers utilize the Darcy-Weisbach equation to calculate pumping head requirements and size booster pump stations. Underestimating $f$ results in undersized pumps unable to deliver required flow pressures to terminal reservoirs.

11. Self-Assessment Conceptual Questions & Model Answers

Q1: Why does aged cast iron pipe exhibit significantly higher head loss than new pipe?
A1: Internal corrosion, tuberculation, and bio-mineral incrustation dramatically increase absolute wall roughness $\epsilon$ from $0.26\text{ mm}$ to over $3.0\text{ mm}$, more than doubling the Darcy friction factor.

Q2: How does air entrainment alter frictional head loss in water pipelines?
A2: Air pockets collect at pipeline high points, reducing effective flow area and creating severe localized throttling losses comparable to partially closed gate valves.

12. Concluding Summary & Verified Engineering Metric

The pressurized conduit friction investigation rigorously validated the Darcy-Weisbach formulation. The verified quadratic resistance factor $k_{pipe} = 0.4200\text{ s}^2\text{/m}$ ($R^2 = 1.000000$) establishes a Darcy friction factor $f = 0.0198$ for smooth copper conduits, providing an authoritative standard for pipeline hydraulic network modeling.

title: Minor Energy Losses in Pipe Fittings, Sudden Expansions, Contractions & Valves
aim: Quantify localized minor energy losses (h_L) and loss coefficients (K_L) across 90° elbows, sudden pipe enlargements, sudden contractions, and globe valves in pressurized pipe flow.
intro: In civil pipeline networks, water treatment piping galleries, building plumbing systems, and fire protection distribution mains, fluids encounter valves, elbows, tees, reducers, and sudden cross-sectional geometry changes that induce flow separation, recirculating vortices, and severe eddy turbulence. Although termed 'minor losses' in contrast to continuous pipe wall friction ('major losses'), these localized disruptions frequently dominate total system head loss in complex plant pipework. Localized minor head loss h_L is formulated in terms of kinetic velocity head: h_L = K_L · (v² / 2g), where K_L is the dimensionless minor loss coefficient. For a sudden enlargement from diameter D_1 to D_2, the Borda-Carnot momentum equation provides an exact analytical loss coefficient: K_L = [1 - (D_1/D_2)²]². For sudden contractions, loss occurs due to flow convergence into a vena contracta followed by turbulent re-expansion (K_L ≈ 0.4 to 0.5). For standard 90° elbows, flow separation along the inner radius and secondary swirling double-vortices produce K_L ≈ 0.75 to 0.90. Fully open globe valves introduce intense tortuous flow redirection (K_L ≈ 5.0 to 10.0), whereas gate valves offer minimal resistance (K_L ≈ 0.15). In this laboratory test rig, multi-port differential manometers record piezometric head drops across standardized pipe fittings across kinetic heads from 0.05 to 0.35 m to determine empirical loss coefficient K_L = 2.4500.
modelExtra: Evaluated on a series piping assembly containing a standard 90° elbow, sudden enlargement, and control valve. Linear model relates localized head loss h_L directly to velocity head v²/(2g) with combined loss slope K_L = 2.4500.

procedure.title: Apparatus Priming & Air Bubble Purging
procedure.text: Start recirculating pump; open bleed valves on all piezometer tubes; purge all air until clear, bubble-free water columns appear in the manometer bank.

procedure.title: Zero Flow Static Datum Check
procedure.text: Close downstream control valve; verify that all piezometer tubes read identical horizontal levels corresponding to static datum.

procedure.title: Flow Adjustment to Initial Velocity Head
procedure.text: Adjust pump speed and throttle valve to establish initial velocity head v²/(2g) = 0.05 m in the reference 25 mm pipe.

procedure.title: Piezometric Head Drop Measurement
procedure.text: Record piezometric levels immediately upstream (h_u) and downstream (h_d) of the test fitting assembly; subtract continuous pipe friction between taps to isolate net minor head loss h_L.

procedure.title: Systematic Velocity Head Escalation
procedure.text: Increase flow across six systematic velocity head steps (0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.20, 0.25, and 0.30 m); log net head loss for each trial.

procedure.title: Minor Loss Coefficient Regression Calculation
procedure.text: Plot minor head loss h_L versus kinetic velocity head v²/(2g); determine linear slope to evaluate empirical loss coefficient K_L.

topics.question: Why are localized fittings losses termed 'minor losses', and when is this terminology misleading?
topics.answer: They are called 'minor' because in long cross-country water transmission pipelines (tens of kilometers), friction losses completely dominate total head loss; however, in short building piping, pump stations, or water treatment plants with hundreds of valves and fittings, 'minor' losses can account for over 80% of total head loss.

topics.question: What is the Borda-Carnot equation and how is it derived for a sudden pipe enlargement?
topics.answer: The Borda-Carnot equation states h_L = (v_1 - v_2)² / (2g) = [1 - (A_1/A_2)]² · (v_1²/2g); it is derived by combining the 1D momentum conservation equation across the expanding jet with the energy equation, assuming hydrostatic wall pressure across the expansion step.

topics.question: Why does a sudden contraction have a lower head loss than a sudden expansion of the same diameter ratio?
topics.answer: In a contraction, flow accelerates smoothly into the smaller section with minimal turbulence; major energy loss occurs only during the subsequent turbulent deceleration from the vena contracta back to the pipe walls, which involves a much smaller turbulent zone than a sudden expansion.

topics.question: What is the physical mechanism causing energy loss in a 90° pipe elbow?
topics.answer: Centrifugal forces push fast-moving fluid toward the outer wall, generating a radial pressure gradient that drives secondary counter-rotating Dean vortices, while boundary layer separation on the inner wall forms a turbulent recirculation wake.

topics.question: How does a globe valve compare to a gate valve in terms of minor loss coefficient K_L?
topics.answer: A fully open gate valve provides a straight, unobstructed circular passage with minimal loss (K_L ≈ 0.15); a globe valve forces water through two 90° turns and across an internal baffle seat, producing severe turbulence and high head loss (K_L ≈ 5.0 to 10.0).

topics.question: What is the equivalent length method for calculating minor losses in piping networks?
topics.answer: The equivalent length method expresses fitting loss as an equivalent length L_e of straight pipe that produces the identical friction loss: L_e = (K_L · D) / f, allowing all fittings to be lumped directly into the Darcy-Weisbach pipe length.

precautions: Purge all air from piezometer manometer tubes before recording static heads to avoid hydrostatic column offsets.
Subtract the linear Darcy-Weisbach friction head loss occurring between pressure tap stations to isolate pure fitting loss.
Ensure pressure taps are located at least 10 pipe diameters downstream of the fitting to allow separated wakes to reattach.
Operate control valves smoothly to prevent water hammer pressure transients from damaging manometer glass tubes.

measureLabel: Record pipe fitting minor head loss
theory:
Mechanics of Localized Fitting Losses

In pressurized piping, sudden changes in boundary geometry cause streamline detachment, creating high-shear mixing zones and recirculating wakes where kinetic energy is dissipated into internal heat through turbulent viscosity. Minor head loss is expressed as:

\[ h_L = K_L \frac{v^2}{2g} \]

where $K_L$ is the minor loss coefficient and $v$ is reference mean velocity (usually in the smaller pipe section).

The Borda-Carnot Sudden Expansion Formulation

Consider a sudden pipe expansion from diameter $D_1$ (area $A_1$, velocity $v_1$) to $D_2$ (area $A_2$, velocity $v_2$). Momentum conservation across the control volume gives:

\[ P_1 A_2 - P_2 A_2 = \rho Q (v_2 - v_1) \]

Dividing by $\rho g A_2$ and substituting continuity $Q = A_2 v_2$:

\[ \frac{P_1 - P_2}{\rho g} = \frac{v_2 (v_2 - v_1)}{g} \]

The energy equation between sections 1 and 2 yields:

\[ h_L = \left( \frac{P_1}{\rho g} + \frac{v_1^2}{2g} \right) - \left( \frac{P_2}{\rho g} + \frac{v_2^2}{2g} \right) = \frac{P_1 - P_2}{\rho g} + \frac{v_1^2 - v_2^2}{2g} \]

Substituting the momentum relation for pressure differential:

\[ h_L = \frac{v_2^2 - v_1 v_2}{g} + \frac{v_1^2 - v_2^2}{2g} = \frac{(v_1 - v_2)^2}{2g} = \left[ 1 - \frac{A_1}{A_2} \right]^2 \frac{v_1^2}{2g} \]

Thus, theoretical loss coefficient for a sudden expansion is $K_{L,exp} = [1 - (D_1/D_2)^2]^2$.
report:
1. Objective & Practical Significance

This laboratory investigation quantified localized minor energy losses and evaluated the composite loss coefficient $K_L$ for a piping assembly containing a standard $90^\circ$ elbow, sudden expansion ($25\text{ mm}$ to $50\text{ mm}$), and control valve across six systematic velocity head levels ($v^2/(2g) = 0.05$ to $0.30\text{ m}$). Findings benchmark hydraulic head loss models used in pump station design.

2. Governing Transport Equations & Energy Conservation

Minor energy losses in pipe fittings scale with kinetic velocity head:

\[ h_L = K_L \frac{v^2}{2g} \]

Linear regression of localized head loss $h_L$ against kinetic velocity head $v^2/(2g)$ yields the empirical loss coefficient $K_L = 2.4500$.

3. Experimental Apparatus & Instrumentation Specification

The test bench comprised a transparent acrylic flow loop incorporating a standard radius $90^\circ$ elbow ($R/D = 1.5$), abrupt enlargement ($D_1 = 25.0\text{ mm}$, $D_2 = 50.0\text{ mm}$), abrupt contraction, and ball valve. Piezometric heads were measured using an array of 14 vertical manometer tubes ($\pm 1.0\text{ mm}$) and an auxiliary Validyne differential pressure transducer. Flow was monitored with an electromagnetic meter.

4. Standard Operating Procedure & Measurement Protocols

The system was primed and de-aired via bleed needle valves. Flow rate was increased systematically across kinetic heads $0.05$ to $0.30\text{ m}$. Static piezometer elevations upstream and downstream of each component were logged. Frictional head loss over the straight pipe length between taps was subtracted to isolate net minor fitting loss $h_L$.

5. Safety Analysis, Hazard Mitigation & Personal Protection

Pressure surges during rapid valve closure can shatter glass manometer columns. Operators adjusted valves slowly to avoid water hammer. Pressure relief valves were set to $3.0\text{ bar}$.

6. Raw Experimental Observations & Systematic Data Records

Simulated demonstration data. The following systematic observations were recorded for reference pipe diameter $D = 25.0\text{ mm}$:

RunVelocity Head v²/(2g) (m)Velocity v (m/s)Discharge Q (L/s)Measured Minor Loss h_L (m)Empirical K_L

20.101.4010.6870.24502.450

7. Quantitative Mathematical Analysis & Regression Models

Linear regression of minor head loss $h_L$ against velocity head $v^2/(2g)$ yields:

\[ h_L = 2.45000 \cdot \left( \frac{v^2}{2g} \right) + 0.00000 \]

with coefficient of determination $R^2 = 1.000000$. The experimental combined minor loss coefficient $K_L = 2.4500$ confirms manufacturer design benchmarks ($0.00\%$ deviation).

8. Rigorous Error Analysis & Uncertainty Propagation

Manometer reading uncertainty is $\delta h = \pm 0.002\text{ m}$, and flow velocity uncertainty is $\delta v = \pm 0.01\text{ m/s}$. Propagating into $K_L$:

\[ \frac{\delta K_L}{K_L} = \sqrt{ \left( \frac{\delta h_L}{h_L} \right)^2 + \left( 2 \frac{\delta v}{v} \right)^2 } = \pm 1.45\% \]

The reported minor loss coefficient is $K_L = 2.450 \pm 0.035$.

9. Engineering Discussion & Phenomenological Interpretation

The linear dependence on velocity head confirmed that energy dissipation in fittings is dominated by turbulent separation vortices. Decomposing the combined coefficient revealed individual contributions: sudden expansion $K_{L,exp} = 0.56$ (Borda-Carnot theoretical $= [1 - (25/50)^2]^2 = 0.563$), $90^\circ$ elbow $K_{L,elbow} = 0.85$, and open valve $K_{L,valve} = 1.04$.

10. Industrial Scale-Up & Pump Station Optimization

In high-capacity water pumping facilities, replacing standard short-radius elbows ($K_L = 0.90$) with long-radius swept bends ($K_L = 0.20$) and full-port ball valves reduces pumping head requirements by up to $15\%$, yielding substantial annual electricity savings.

11. Self-Assessment Conceptual Questions & Model Answers

Q1: Why does a gradual conical diffuser reduce head loss compared to a sudden enlargement?
A1: A gradual diffuser with expansion angle $2\theta \approx 7^\circ$ to $8^\circ$ maintains adverse pressure gradients low enough to prevent boundary layer separation, reducing loss coefficient from $K_L \approx 0.56$ down to $0.15$.

Q2: How does secondary flow in pipe bends cause premature internal pipe erosion?
A2: High-velocity centrifugal fluid impinges on the outer elbow wall, eroding the protective oxide scale and causing flow-accelerated corrosion (FAC) wall thinning.

12. Concluding Summary & Verified Engineering Metric

The pipe fitting minor loss investigation confirmed that localized head losses scale with kinetic velocity head. The verified composite loss coefficient $K_L = 2.4500$ ($R^2 = 1.000000$) validates the Borda-Carnot formulation and provides accurate loss parameters for hydraulic network modeling.

title: Coagulation-Flocculation Optimization & Residual Turbidity via Standard Jar Test
aim: Determine the optimum coagulant dosage (alum / polyaluminum chloride) and rapid/slow mixing conditions for maximum turbidity and suspended colloidal particle removal from raw surface water according to ASTM D2035.
targetName: Turbidity Removal Rate per Unit Coagulant
intro: In civil environmental water treatment engineering, raw surface waters from rivers and reservoirs contain suspended silt, clay, pathogenic microorganisms, and natural organic matter (NOM) present as negatively charged microscopic colloids (0.001 to 1.0 µm). Due to electrostatic repulsion governed by negative zeta potentials (-15 to -30 mV), colloidal particles remain indefinitely suspended in stable Brownian motion and cannot settle by gravity alone. Coagulation and flocculation destabilize this colloidal suspension. Developed in the 1920s, the standard Jar Test (ASTM D2035) uses a multi-paddle stirrer to optimize chemical dosing in municipal water treatment plants. Adding hydrolyzing metal coagulants—such as aluminum sulfate (alum, Al₂(SO₄)₃·14H₂O) or ferric chloride (FeCl₃)—destabilizes colloids through two primary mechanisms: (1) Charge neutralization: trivalent cations (Al³⁺, Al(OH)²⁺, Al₇(OH)₁₇⁴⁺) compress the electrical diffuse double layer and neutralize negative surface charges; and (2) Sweep flocculation: at higher dosages and neutral pH (6.5 to 7.5), amorphous aluminum hydroxide Al(OH)₃ precipitates en masse, physically entrapping and sweeping suspended particles into settleable flocs. In this laboratory experiment, six 1-liter water samples are dosed with alum from 10 to 40 mg/L, subjected to 1-minute rapid mixing (100 rpm), 20-minute slow flocculation (30 rpm), and 30-minute quiescent settling to calibrate residual turbidity reduction and establish the optimum economic dosage.
modelExtra: Tested on synthetic turbid river water (initial turbidity = 48.0 NTU, pH = 7.2, alkalinity = 85 mg/L as CaCO3). Linearized regression over the sub-optimal to optimal dose range correlates residual turbidity to alum dose with slope -0.8500 NTU/(mg/L).
